# Specification: `parse_iso8601_duration(s)`

## 1. Normative reference & conventions ledger
Base document: **ISO 8601-1:2019**, duration production `P[nY][nM][nD][T[nH][nM][nS]]` plus the alternative week form `PnW`. ISO 8601-2:2019 sign/negative extensions are **rejected**. Every contested feature is pinned explicitly so no decision is left to reader inference:

| Feature | Adopted | Rejected alternative | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| Signs / negatives (`-P1D`, `P-1D`, `P+1D`, `+`) | none | 8601-2 leading/per-component signs | base 8601-1 has no sign |
| Decimal separator | both `.` and `,` (comma normalized to `.`) | dot-only (RFC-3339 house style) | ISO permits comma; **interpretive** |
| Fraction placement | least-significant (last-present) component **only**, ≥1 ASCII digit on **both** sides | any component; seconds-only | ISO "smallest value may carry a fraction" |
| Bare/trailing separator (`PT1.S`, `PT.5S`, `P0.S`) | reject → `MalformedNumber` | tolerate | fraction needs digits both sides |
| Week form `PnW` | mutually exclusive with all other designators | mixable (`P1W1D`) | ISO week form is standalone |
| Fractional week (`P1.5W`) | accept | reject | W is the sole/last component; **interpretive** |
| Digit set | ASCII `[0-9]` only | Unicode Nd (Arabic-Indic, fullwidth) | `int()`/`Decimal()` silently absorb Nd |
| Designator case | uppercase ASCII only | case-insensitive | ISO designators are uppercase |
| Cross-unit carry | **none**; each component preserved as parsed | roll `90m→1h30m`, `1W→7D`, `1M→30D` | month/year/week/day lengths are calendar-dependent (DST/leap) — carry would assert false durations |
| Magnitude | **bounded**: `MAX_DIGITS` (default 4096) per numeric token; over → `Overflow` | unbounded arbitrary precision | deterministic, resource-bounded, keeps totality airtight (see §6) |
| Input domain | all Python objects | str-only with incidental `TypeError` | outcome must be *defined* |

## 2. Input domain & output structure
**Domain:** all Python objects — the function is total over `object`. **Output on accept:** an immutable record
`Duration(years, months, weeks, days, hours, minutes, seconds)`, each a `decimal.Decimal`, default `Decimal(0)`. Canonical zero = all seven fields `Decimal(0)`. `Decimal` is chosen for exact fractions and exact large integers (float would corrupt `0.1`); ISO fractions are decimal, so `Decimal` is exact. **At most one field is fractional** (§1). The week form sets only `weeks`; non-week forms leave `weeks == 0`. `weeks` is a first-class field precisely because it is **not** expanded to days. A zero-valued component (`P0D`) is a *present component* → accepted with that field `Decimal(0)`.

## 3. Grammar (anchored, ASCII, case-sensitive)
ABNF (RFC 5234), whole-string match:
```
duration   = "P" ( week-form / dt-form )
week-form  = number "W"
dt-form    = date-part [ "T" time-part ]     ; date-part and time-part each ≥1 component (side cond)
date-part  = [ number "Y" ] [ number "M" ] [ number "D" ]
time-part  = [ number "H" ] [ number "M" ] [ number "S" ]
number     = 1*DIGIT [ ("." / ",") 1*DIGIT ]
DIGIT      = %x30-39                          ; ASCII only
```
By construction: `P` mandatory; date order fixed Y,M,D and time order fixed H,M,S (out-of-order cannot whole-match); the `M` month/minute ambiguity is resolved **positionally by the unique `T` delimiter** (`M` before `T` = months, after = minutes) for every string; the week branch is a separate alternative so `W` cannot co-occur with other designators; `number` forbids bare/trailing separators. Implementation recognizer (a single anchored regex with `[0-9]` — **never `\d`**, which would match Unicode Nd):
```
^P(?:([0-9]+(?:[.,][0-9]+)?)W|(?:([0-9]+(?:[.,][0-9]+)?)Y)?(?:([0-9]+(?:[.,][0-9]+)?)M)?(?:([0-9]+(?:[.,][0-9]+)?)D)?(?:T(?:([0-9]+(?:[.,][0-9]+)?)H)?(?:([0-9]+(?:[.,][0-9]+)?)M)?(?:([0-9]+(?:[.,][0-9]+)?)S)?)?)$
```
The recognizer is intentionally permissive about two things (it *matches* `P` and `PT`, and does not itself enforce fraction-position); these are closed by the ordered predicates in §5, not by the regex.

## 4. Error taxonomy
Root `ISO8601DurationError(ValueError)` with members: `EmptyInput, MissingPrefix, SignedValue, NonAsciiDigit, LowercaseDesignator, InvalidCharacter, Overflow, NoComponents, BareTimeDesignator, MissingTimeDesignator, MisplacedFraction, MalformedNumber, WeekWithOtherComponents, BadDesignatorOrder, InvalidSyntax` (catch-all). Separately, non-`str` input raises `TypeError`, outside the `ValueError` tree. Every rejection maps to exactly one member.

## 5. Decision procedure (ordered; first firing gate wins)
This ordering is chosen so that every input with *overlapping* defects resolves deterministically to one outcome.
- **G0** `not isinstance(s, str)` → **TypeError**. (`str` subclasses admitted; `bytes`/`bytearray` are non-str → TypeError, never implicitly decoded.)
- **G1** `s == ""` → **EmptyInput**.
- **G2** `s[0]` is `+` or `-` → **SignedValue**. *(Placed before the prefix check so `-P1D`/`+P1D` route to SignedValue, not MissingPrefix.)*
- **G3** `s[0] != 'P'` → **MissingPrefix**. *(A leading lowercase `p` or leading space lands here — see honest note below.)*
- **G4 alphabet gate** (before any numeric parse) scan `s[1:]`; classify the **first** offending code point by fixed priority: a Unicode decimal digit that is not ASCII → **NonAsciiDigit**; an ASCII lowercase designator letter `p t y m w d h s` → **LowercaseDesignator**; any other disallowed char (space, `_`, other letters) → **InvalidCharacter**.
- **G5 magnitude** any numeric token whose integer- or fraction-part length `> MAX_DIGITS` → **Overflow**. *(Checked before `Decimal` construction, so no `MemoryError` can escape on astronomically long inputs.)*
- **G6** match `s` against the §3 recognizer:
  - **Week-form match** → build `Duration(weeks=…)`; accept.
  - **dt-form match** → ordered predicates, first-fire:
    - no component present: if `'T' in s` → **BareTimeDesignator** (`PT`) else → **NoComponents** (`P`). *(This single ordered test resolves the `PT` "empty-components vs bare-T" overlap deterministically.)*
    - `'T'` present but zero H/M/S → **BareTimeDesignator** (`P1DT`).
    - a present component other than the last-present carries a fraction → **MisplacedFraction** (`P1.5Y2M`).
    - else build `Duration`; accept.
  - **No match** → diagnosis, in order (each predicate first requires that all numeric tokens are well-formed `[0-9]+([.,][0-9]+)?`; a malformed token → **MalformedNumber**, which routes `PT.5S`/`PT1.S`/`P0.S` correctly and prevents the crude "S-without-T" misroute): `'W'` present alongside any other designator → **WeekWithOtherComponents** (`P1W1D`, `P1Y2W`); well-formed `H`/`M`/`S` component with no preceding `'T'` → **MissingTimeDesignator** (`P1H`); valid designators not in strictly-canonical unique order (out-of-order or repeated) → **BadDesignatorOrder** (`P1D1Y`, `P1Y1Y`); else → **InvalidSyntax**.

## 6. Master case table (this table *is* the totality argument)
| Input class | Example | Outcome |
|---|---|---|
| non-str | `None`, `b"P1D"`, `5` | TypeError |
| empty | `""` | EmptyInput |
| signed / negative | `-P1D`, `P-1D`, `P+1D` | SignedValue |
| missing P / leading lowercase p / leading space | `1Y2M`, `p1d`, `pt0s`, ` P1D` | MissingPrefix |
| unicode digits | `P１D`, `P٢D` | NonAsciiDigit |
| interior lowercase | `P1d`, `PT1s` | LowercaseDesignator |
| interior whitespace/underscore | `P1 D`, `P1_D` | InvalidCharacter |
| overflow magnitude | `P` + `9`×10⁶ + `D` | Overflow |
| P alone | `P` | NoComponents |
| bare T | `PT`, `P1DT` | BareTimeDesignator |
| time comp without T | `P1H`, `P1S` | MissingTimeDesignator |
| out-of-order / repeated | `P1D1Y`, `P1Y1Y`, `PT1S1H` | BadDesignatorOrder |
| fraction not on smallest | `P1.5Y2M`, `P1Y1.5DT1S` | MisplacedFraction |
| degenerate separator | `PT.5S`, `PT1.S`, `P0.S` | MalformedNumber |
| week + other | `P1W1D`, `P1Y2W` | WeekWithOtherComponents |
| other residue | `P1`, `P1..2D` | InvalidSyntax |
| **accept: full** | `P3Y6M4DT12H30M5S` | y3 m6 d4 h12 min30 s5, no carry |
| **accept: zero** | `PT0S`, `P0D`, `P0Y0M0D` | zero-valued present components |
| **accept: week** | `P1W`, `P1.5W` | weeks=1 / weeks=1.5 |
| **accept: no-carry** | `PT90M` | minutes=90 (NOT 1h30m) |
| **accept: leading zeros** | `P01D` | days=1 |
| **accept: fraction on smallest** | `PT1.5S`, `P1,5D` | seconds=1.5 / days=1.5 |
| **accept: positional M** | `P1M` / `PT1M` | months=1 / minutes=1 |

## 7. Totality argument
`object = non-str ⊎ str`; non-str → TypeError (G0). For a string, G1–G6 form a finite ordered chain; the **first** firing gate wins, so an input with several defects (e.g. lowercase *and* out-of-order) maps deterministically to the earliest gate — exactly one outcome, no overlap. G6's recognizer is a whole-string match over a finite alphabet: **match** → the ordered accept-predicates each emit exactly one of {ACCEPT, NoComponents, BareTimeDesignator, MisplacedFraction}; **no-match** → the ordered diagnosis ends in the **InvalidSyntax catch-all**, so no string escapes classification. Every predicate is bounded by `|s|`; the G5 magnitude guard bounds `Decimal` construction (so even a 10⁶-digit input terminates with `Overflow`, never a `MemoryError`). Hence `parse_iso8601_duration` is defined, single-valued, and terminating on every possible input — a total decision procedure with no undefined region.

## 8. Honest notes
- Routing a leading lowercase `p`, leading sign, or leading space at G2/G3 is a *diagnosis-label* choice; the string is rejected either way, so correctness does not depend on it. The labels above are the ones the stated gate order actually produces.
- Comma-as-separator, fraction-on-last-only, and fractional-week acceptance are ISO 8601-1-conforming but a stricter house style (dot-only, seconds-only fractions, reject `P1.5W`) is equally defensible — flip the corresponding ledger rows without disturbing the totality proof.
- The bounded-magnitude policy (`Overflow`) is chosen over unbounded arbitrary precision because unbounded precision leaves a `MemoryError` escape that would silently break totality on pathological inputs; the exact `MAX_DIGITS` is a policy dial.

arms.answer:
## Fibonacci heaps vs. pairing heaps for Dijkstra

Dijkstra with a decrease-key–based priority queue issues exactly three kinds of PQ operations on a graph with V vertices, E edges: **V inserts**, **V extract‑mins**, and **at most E decrease‑keys** (one relaxation per edge; find‑min is folded into extract‑min). meld/union is not used, so I omit it except to note both heaps do it in O(1). The overall bound is obtained by summing *amortized* costs, which is legitimate: amortized bounds hold for any operation sequence, and because the potential starts at 0 (empty heap) and ends ≥ 0, total actual work ≤ total amortized work even though the operations are interleaved.

### 1. Per‑operation costs

**Fibonacci heap** (Fredman & Tarjan, 1987). Potential Φ = t + 2m, where t = #trees in the root list, m = #marked nodes.

| op | worst‑case (single op) | amortized |
|---|---|---|
| insert | O(1) | O(1) |
| find‑min | O(1) | O(1) |
| decrease‑key | Θ(cascade length); not O(1) — up to O(n) adversarially | **O(1)** |
| extract‑min | O(n) (consolidation of up to n roots) | **O(log n)** |

**Pairing heap** (Fredman, Sedgewick, Sleator & Tarjan, 1986). Analyzed via a similar amortized/potential argument on subtree sizes.

| op | worst‑case (single op) | amortized |
|---|---|---|
| insert | O(1) | O(1) (Iacono 2000: O(1) amortized proven) |
| find‑min | O(1) | O(1) |
| decrease‑key | **O(1) actual** (detach subtree, one comparison; work deferred) | **not O(1)**: between Ω(log log n) (Fredman 1999 lower bound) and O(2^{2√(log log n)}) (Pettie 2005); the classic 1986 analysis gives O(log n) |
| extract‑min | O(n) (two‑pass melding of up to n children) | O(log n) |

Note the striking role reversal on decrease‑key: the **Fibonacci heap does potentially large actual work but is O(1) amortized**, whereas the **pairing heap does O(1) actual work but is provably ω(1) amortized** — its cost is a deferred restructuring charge paid at the next extract‑min.

### 2. Dijkstra bound derivation

**Fibonacci:**
- V inserts × O(1) = O(V)
- V extract‑mins × O(log V) = O(V log V)
- E decrease‑keys × O(1) = O(E)
- **Total: O(E + V log V).**

This is the landmark Fredman–Tarjan result; it is asymptotically optimal for comparison‑based Dijkstra with a general PQ, and dominates the binary‑heap bound O(E log V) whenever E = ω(V).

**Pairing (using the simple O(log V) decrease‑key analysis):**
- V inserts = O(V)
- V extract‑mins = O(V log V)
- E decrease‑keys × O(log V) = O(E log V)
- **Total: O(E log V)** (for a connected graph E ≥ V−1, so this term absorbs V log V).

Using Pettie’s tighter bound the decrease‑key term shrinks to O(E · 2^{2√(log log V)}), giving **O(V log V + E·2^{2√(log log V)})** — strictly between the two above: better than O(E log V), but never as good as Fibonacci’s O(E + V log V), because pairing’s decrease‑key cannot be O(1).

### 3. Where each wins — precisely

**By density (theory):**
- **Sparse, E = Θ(V):** Fibonacci = O(V log V); pairing = O(E log V) = O(V log V). **Tie asymptotically.** Decrease‑key is not the bottleneck (only O(V) of them dominate nothing), so Fibonacci’s O(1) decrease‑key buys nothing here. Even a binary heap gives O(V log V). The heap choice is asymptotically irrelevant on sparse graphs.
- **Dense, E = Θ(V²):** Fibonacci = O(V² + V log V) = O(V²) = **O(E), optimal** (you must inspect every edge). Pairing = O(V² log V) = O(E log V), a full log factor worse. **This is exactly where Fibonacci’s theoretical advantage is maximal**, because decrease‑key is now the dominant operation (Θ(V²) of them vs. only V extract‑mins), and it is the operation Fibonacci makes free.

**Theory vs. practice:**
- **Theory: Fibonacci wins.** O(E + V log V) is the asymptotically best comparison‑based Dijkstra bound achievable with this operation set, and pairing *provably* cannot match it — Fredman (1999) showed any pairing‑heap‑like self‑adjusting heap needs Ω(log log n) amortized decrease‑key, so the E·(something growing) term is unavoidable.
- **Practice: pairing wins, almost always.** Fibonacci heaps carry huge constant factors and terrible cache locality: every node stores parent/child/left/right sibling pointers plus a degree and a mark bit, and each operation touches the mark machinery, cascading cuts, and consolidation via a degree‑indexed array. Pairing heap nodes are leaner and pointer‑chase less; their decrease‑key is a two‑pointer splice, and empirically behaves like O(1). Empirical studies consistently confirm this: Stasko & Vitter (1987), Moret & Shapiro (1991), and Larkin, Sen & Tarjan (2014, "A Back‑to‑Basics Empirical Study") all find pairing heaps beating Fibonacci heaps on Dijkstra — and Larkin–Sen–Tarjan further find that a simple implicit d‑ary/binary heap, especially with decrease‑key replaced by *lazy deletion* (insert a fresh entry and skip stale pops, giving O(E log V) with no decrease‑key at all), often beats both pointer‑based heaps on real inputs because of cache behavior. So the constant‑factor and memory‑hierarchy realities invert the asymptotic ranking.

**Summary rule of thumb:** choose Fibonacci only when the graph is dense *and* asymptotic worst‑case guarantees genuinely matter; for essentially all practical Dijkstra, use a pairing heap or a d‑ary heap with lazy deletion.

### 4. The single most subtle point in the amortized decrease‑key argument — and the correct statement

The point most often stated incorrectly is the meaning of "decrease‑key is O(1)" for the **Fibonacci heap**. It is routinely paraphrased as "decrease‑key does O(1) work," which is **false**: a single decrease‑key triggers a cascade of cuts and does Θ(c) actual work, where c is the number of consecutive marked ancestors on the path to the root — Θ(log n) typically and up to Θ(n) in adversarial sequences. Only the **amortized** cost is O(1).

Stated correctly, and pinning down *why*: let a decrease‑key perform c cuts (the target node x plus c−1 cascading cuts of marked ancestors), then mark one previously‑unmarked node. With Φ = t + 2m:
- trees increase by c (each cut node becomes a new root): Δt = +c;
- marks change by Δm = −(c−1) + 1 = 2 − c.

So ΔΦ = c + 2(2 − c) = 4 − c, and amortized = actual + ΔΦ = c + (4 − c) = 4 = O(1).

The subtlety lives entirely in the **coefficient 2 on marked nodes**, and it is the part people get wrong or gloss over. Each marked node is carrying *two* prepaid credits, and both are needed: **one credit pays for the actual O(1) cost of cutting that node when the cascade eventually reaches it, and the second credit cancels the +1 increase in the tree‑count potential caused when that cut turns the node into a new root.** If you (as many informal accounts implicitly do) use coefficient 1, the algebra gives ΔΦ = c + (2 − c) = 2 and amortized = c + 2 = O(c) — the analysis collapses, because a single released mark‑credit cannot simultaneously pay for the cut *and* absorb the new tree. The correct one‑sentence statement is therefore:

> *Fibonacci decrease‑key is O(1) amortized, not O(1) actual; a single call can do work proportional to a long chain of cascading cuts, and that work is financed by potential prepaid on marked nodes at rate 2 per mark — one unit for the future cut itself, one unit to neutralize the tree‑count increase that cut produces — which is exactly why the factor must be 2.*

A closely related and equally common error, on the pairing‑heap side, is asserting that pairing decrease‑key is O(1) amortized (the original 1986 conjecture). It is not: Fredman’s 1999 Ω(log log n) lower bound refutes it, and the current best upper bound is Pettie’s O(2^{2√(log log n)}). What *is* O(1) for a pairing heap is the **actual** work of decrease‑key — the exact mirror image of the Fibonacci situation.

# Fibonacci Heaps vs Pairing Heaps for Dijkstra

## 1. Per-operation costs (heap size n; for Dijkstra n ≤ V)

### Fibonacci heap (Fredman–Tarjan 1984/87)

| Operation | Amortized | Worst case (single op) |
|---|---|---|
| insert | O(1) | O(1) |
| find-min | O(1) | O(1) |
| decrease-key | **O(1)** | **Θ(n)** — a cascading-cut chain can be forced to linear length (Fibonacci heaps can be driven into linear chains, cf. CLRS Problem 19-4, with long runs of marked ancestors) |
| extract-min | O(log n) | Θ(n) — consolidation may touch Θ(n) roots |
| meld | O(1) | O(1) |

Potential function: Φ(H) = t(H) + 2·m(H), where t = number of root trees, m = number of marked nodes.

The size invariant that makes extract-min O(log n) amortized: a node of degree d roots a subtree of size ≥ F(d+2) ≥ φ^d, so max degree D(n) = O(log n) (base φ ≈ 1.618, i.e., log_φ n ≈ 1.44 lg n). This invariant holds *because* the mark/cascading-cut rule guarantees each node loses at most one child between the time it is linked under a parent and the time it is itself cut — hence the i-th child of any node has degree ≥ i − 2 (not i − 1, as in binomial heaps).

If per-operation worst-case bounds matter (real-time systems), the strict Fibonacci heap (Brodal–Lagogiannis–Tarjan 2012) and Brodal queues (1996) achieve the same bounds worst-case per operation, at substantial constant-factor cost.

### Pairing heap (Fredman–Sedgewick–Sleator–Tarjan 1986)

| Operation | Amortized | Worst case (single op) |
|---|---|---|
| insert | O(1) (Iacono 2000; original FSST analysis gave O(log n)) | O(1) |
| find-min | O(1) | O(1) |
| decrease-key | **open**: between **Ω(log log n)** (Fredman 1999 lower bound) and **O(log n)** (FSST); Pettie 2005 shows O(4^{√(log log n)}) = o(log^ε n) when insert/meld share that bound | **O(1) actual** (detach subtree, link with root) |
| extract-min | O(log n) | Θ(n) — two-pass pairing over up to n children |
| meld | O(1)–O(log n) amortized depending on analysis | O(1) |

Note the exact inversion of the trap for decrease-key: Fibonacci is O(1) *amortized* but Θ(n) worst-case single-op; pairing is O(1) *worst-case actual* but provably **not** O(1) amortized — the cheap cut leaves structural damage (loss of "heap-ordered tournament" information) that later extract-mins must pay for. FSST conjectured O(1) amortized; Fredman disproved it in a model that captures standard pairing heaps and their generalizations.

## 2. Dijkstra bound derivation

Operation counts: exactly V inserts (or ≤ V with lazy insertion), V extract-mins, ≤ E decrease-keys (at most one per edge relaxation, ≤ 1 per directed edge).

Because amortized costs telescope over any operation sequence starting from an empty heap, the summed amortized costs are a **genuine worst-case bound on total time** — a point that matters: no "the input might hit the Θ(n) op repeatedly" objection applies to the total.

- **Fibonacci:** V·O(1) + E·O(1) + V·O(log V) = **O(E + V log V)**. This is optimal for comparison-based Dijkstra with decrease-key. (For integer weights, RAM algorithms do better — Thorup, Fredman–Willard — but that's outside both heaps.)
- **Pairing (proven bound):** V·O(1) + E·O(log V) + V·O(log V) = **O((E + V) log V) = O(E log V)** for connected graphs. With Pettie's analysis: **O(E·4^{√(log log V)} + V log V)**.
- Fredman's Ω(log log n) amortized lower bound implies no analysis of the standard pairing heap can ever deliver O(E + V log V); the best conceivable is roughly O(E log log V + V log V). (Careful caveat: the lower bound is over adversarial operation sequences in Fredman's model; it rules out an O(1)-amortized-decrease-key *analysis*, which is what the Dijkstra derivation would need.)

## 3. Where each wins — precisely

**Theory (asymptotics):**
- E = O(V) (sparse): both are Θ(V log V). Fibonacci buys nothing — even a binary heap's O(E log V) = O(V log V) already ties.
- E = ω(V): Fibonacci strictly wins under the proven pairing bound. E.g. E = Θ(V log V): O(V log V) vs O(V log² V). E = Θ(V²) (dense): O(V²) vs O(V² log V) — and even against the Fredman-optimal hypothetical, O(V²) vs Ω(V² log log V).
- Crossover rule of thumb: Fibonacci's advantage is exactly the regime where the E·(decrease-key cost) term dominates V log V, i.e., E/V = ω(1). The denser the graph, the bigger the win.
- Degenerate dense case: for E = Θ(V²), the trivial array + linear-scan Dijkstra is also O(V²), matching Fibonacci with far smaller constants.

**Practice:** pairing heaps win almost universally.
- Fibonacci node: 4 pointers (parent, child, left, right sibling) + degree + mark bit; cascading-cut and consolidation bookkeeping; poor cache locality; constants typically 2–4× worse. Pairing node: 2–3 pointers (left-child/right-sibling + prev/parent), trivially simple code.
- Empirical studies (Stasko–Vitter 1987; Moret–Shapiro 1991; Larkin–Sen–Tarjan 2014 "back-to-basics") consistently rank pairing heaps at or near the top among decrease-key-supporting heaps and Fibonacci heaps well behind; implicit binary/4-ary heaps win outright when decrease-key is rare or eliminated.
- Structural reason the theoretical gap rarely bites: real Dijkstra runs execute far fewer than E decrease-keys (on random graphs the expected count is O(V log(E/V)), and on road networks it is tiny), so the E-term Fibonacci optimizes is mostly hypothetical. Many production codes skip decrease-key entirely (lazy deletion: re-insert and discard stale pops), giving O(E log E) with an implicit heap — usually the fastest of all in practice.
- Net: use Fibonacci heaps to *state* the O(E + V log V) bound; use pairing heaps (or a 4-ary implicit heap / lazy deletion) to *run* Dijkstra.

## 4. The single most subtle point in the decrease-key potential argument — and its correct statement

**The common incorrect statement:** "The marked nodes' potential pays for the cascading cuts, so Φ = (#trees) + (#marked nodes) gives O(1) amortized decrease-key."

**Why it's wrong:** with coefficient 1 on marks the argument collapses. A decrease-key performing c cascading cuts does Θ(c + 1) actual work, creates c + 1 new roots (Δt = +(c+1)), unmarks c nodes, and marks at most one node (the first unmarked non-root ancestor where the cascade stops — the source of the "+1"). Under Φ = t + m, ΔΦ = (c+1) + (−c + 1) = +2: the potential released by unmarking is *exactly cancelled* by the tree-potential increase from the new roots, the amortized cost is Θ(c), and O(1) fails.

**The correct statement:** each unit of mark potential must pay for **two** distinct debts, which is why the potential is Φ = t + **2**m. When a marked node is cascade-cut, its released 2 units cover (i) the O(1) actual work of performing that cut, **and** (ii) the +1 increase in tree potential from the root it just became — i.e., it prepays that root's future handling in extract-min's consolidation. Then ΔΦ = (c+1) + 2(−c + 1) = 3 − c, and amortized cost ≤ Θ(c+1) + (3 − c) (after scaling the potential unit to the cut cost) = O(1). The decrease-key analysis is thus not self-contained: its O(1) is an accounting transfer that keeps extract-min's O(log V) honest — and the mark-after-two-losses rule is simultaneously what preserves size(x) ≥ F(d+2), so cutting eagerly on the first child loss (no marks) breaks the analysis (every cut would cascade to the root with nothing to pay for it), while never cutting breaks the Θ(log n) degree bound that extract-min needs.

Two adjacent traps worth naming because they are stated wrong nearly as often: (a) "Fibonacci decrease-key is O(1)" without the word *amortized* — a single call can cost Θ(n); the guarantee is only on totals over a sequence (which is exactly why the Dijkstra total bound is still worst-case valid); (b) the mirror-image error for pairing heaps — their decrease-key really is O(1) *per call*, yet no potential function can make it O(1) *amortized* (Fredman's Ω(log log n)), because the O(1) cut increases potential rather than decreasing it.

## Fibonacci vs Pairing Heaps for Dijkstra

### 0. The amortization contract (used throughout)
Amortized cost is defined by a potential Φ with Φ(initial)=0 and Φ≥0. For op i with actual cost cᵢ, amortized âᵢ := cᵢ + (Φᵢ − Φᵢ₋₁). Telescoping over a sequence: Σâᵢ = Σcᵢ + Φ_final ≥ Σcᵢ. So amortized costs upper-bound the *total* actual cost over a sequence and say nothing about any *single* call. This wedge between "amortized" and "worst-case-per-op" is the whole story below. Fibonacci-heap bounds use Φ = t(H) + 2·m(H) (number of root-list trees + twice the number of marked nodes), as in CLRS Ch. 19.

### 1. Per-operation costs (amortized | worst-case single call)

**Fibonacci heap**

| op | amortized | worst-case single call |
|---|---|---|
| insert | O(1) | O(1) |
| extract-min | O(log n) | Θ(n) |
| decrease-key | **O(1)** | **Θ(n)** |

- extract-min is O(log n) only *amortized*; right after n inserts the root list has n trees and one consolidation is Θ(n).
- decrease-key's Θ(n) worst case is *real immediate work*: a cascading cut can climb a marked chain of length Θ(n) during the call.

**Pairing heap** (standard two-pass variant)

| op | amortized | worst-case single call |
|---|---|---|
| insert | O(1) (Iacono 2000) | O(1) |
| delete-min | O(log n) | Θ(n) |
| decrease-key | **NOT O(1)** — clean provable bound O(log n) | **O(1)** |

Key contrast (and a point two common write-ups get wrong): a pairing-heap decrease-key does only **O(1) actual work** — detach the node's subtree and one compare-link back at the root. Unlike Fibonacci, it *defers* the restructuring into the next delete-min's combine pass rather than paying it during the call. So its worst-case single call is O(1); the difficulty is entirely in the *amortized/charged* cost.

Historical/precise status of pairing decrease-key: FSST 1986 *proved* O(log n) for all ops and *conjectured* O(1) amortized decrease-key. The conjecture is false: Fredman (1999) proved a super-constant lower bound (Ω(log log n)-order) — **in a restricted generalized-pairing-heap model**, so decrease-key is ω(1); Pettie (2005) gave the best known upper bound ≈ O(2^(2√(log log n))) = o(log n). The exact complexity of the *standard* pairing heap remains open. Confidence: high on "ω(1) and o(log n)"; medium on the exact Pettie exponent and Fredman's model wording (recalled from memory, not re-verified against source in this pass).

### 2. Dijkstra derivation
Op multiset: **V inserts, V extract-mins, ≤ E decrease-keys** (one per relaxed edge). Heap size n ≤ V ⇒ log n = O(log V). Since Φ₀=0 and Φ≥0, summed amortized costs upper-bound the true total, so we substitute amortized costs directly:

- **Fibonacci:** V·O(1) + V·O(log V) + E·O(1) = **O(E + V log V)**.
- **Pairing (clean provable bound):** V·O(1) + V·O(log V) + E·O(log V) = **O(E log V)**.

The comparison hinges entirely on the E-term: to keep the E-weighted contribution linear you need **O(1) amortized decrease-key**. Fibonacci delivers it; pairing provably cannot. (With Pettie's bound, pairing is O(V log V + E·2^(2√(log log V))) — better than E log V, still not O(E + V log V).)

### 3. Where each wins

**By density (asymptotics):**
- **Dense, E = Θ(V²):** Fibonacci O(V²) vs pairing O(V² log V), binary heap O(V² log V). Fibonacci beats the *other heaps* by a log factor. Important caveat: O(V²) is not a unique Fibonacci advantage on dense graphs — a trivial unsorted-array/linear-scan priority queue also gives Θ(V²), which is optimal since any SSSP must read Ω(E)=Ω(V²) edges. So the honest claim is "Fibonacci wins the dense regime *among heap-based implementations*," not "Fibonacci uniquely wins dense graphs."
- **Sparse, E = Θ(V):** Fibonacci, pairing, and binary heaps all give O(V log V). No asymptotic advantage for Fibonacci.
- **Crossover (comparator matters):** Relative to an O(E log V) baseline (binary heap, or pairing under the clean provable bound), Fibonacci's O(E + V log V) is asymptotically strictly better once **E = ω(V)** (full log-factor gap at E = Θ(V²)); at E = Θ(V) they tie. This threshold is stated *against the O(E log V) baseline*. It does NOT hold against a Pettie-optimized pairing heap: there exist densities E = ω(V) (e.g. E ≈ V log V / 2^(2√(log log V))) where both variants are Θ(V log V), so no clean "Fibonacci strictly wins for all E=ω(V)" statement survives if the comparator is best-known pairing rather than a binary heap.

**Theory vs practice (the correct headline — the verdicts invert):**
- **Theory:** Fibonacci is best (unique O(E + V log V); log-factor better than other heaps on dense graphs).
- **Practice:** Pairing heaps are typically *faster*, and for sparse graphs a plain binary/d-ary heap often beats both. Reasons: Fibonacci nodes carry parent + child + two sibling pointers + a degree field + a **mark bit** (heavy memory and pointer surgery); consolidation and cascading cuts chase pointers across scattered memory (poor cache locality) and rarely encounter the long cascades the worst case guards against — large hidden constants. Pairing nodes are leaner (no mark bit, no rank bookkeeping), with better locality and simpler code. So: **theory says Fibonacci, practice says pairing (or a binary heap for sparse E).** (Empirical claim rests on well-known benchmark studies; exact outcomes depend on graph shape, implementation, and platform.)

### 4. The single most-often-mis-stated subtlety in the decrease-key potential argument

**The common surface error:** writing "Fibonacci decrease-key is O(1)" and dropping *amortized* — implying a per-call guarantee, when a single call is Θ(n). That is the most *frequent* mistake, but it is a generic property of all amortized analysis, not a subtlety internal to *this* argument.

**The single load-bearing subtlety, stated correctly (the deepest point most write-ups botch):** the O(1) amortized closes *only* because of the **factor of 2 on marked nodes in Φ = t + 2m**, and **marking exists to bound tree degree — not to make decrease-key cheap.**

Accounting: a decrease-key doing c cuts has actual cost Θ(c). It creates c new root-list trees (Δt = +c). Of the c cuts, the c−1 *cascading* cuts each take a **marked** node, move it to the root list, and **unmark** it (Δm = −(c−1) + 1 for at most one newly marked stopping node = −c+2). So ΔΦ = Δt + 2·Δm = c + 2(−c+2) = **4 − c**, and amortized = Θ(c) + (4−c) = **O(1)**. The two units banked when a node is first marked do double duty — one pays the eventual cut's actual work, the other pays for the +1 tree that cut node becomes on reaching the root list. With a coefficient of 1 the +c and −c would not cancel and the cascade would not telescope. (Honest caveat: the coefficient 2 is what makes *this standard CLRS-style* proof work; it is a proof-specific constant, not the unique value admitting *any* valid amortized analysis.)

The most-mis-*motivated* half: **marking does not accelerate decrease-key — cascading makes a single decrease-key cost more.** Its actual job is to guarantee each non-root loses at most one child before being cut, which forces size(x) ≥ F_(deg(x)+2) ≥ φ^(deg(x)), hence maximum degree D(n) = O(log_φ n) — the exact Fibonacci-number recurrence that also bounds AVL-tree height. *That* degree bound is what keeps **extract-min** consolidation at O(log n). The design deliberately trades away decrease-key's per-op worst case (Θ(n)) to protect extract-min's O(log n) amortized cost.

In one sentence: **decrease-key is O(1) amortized, not worst-case (a single call is Θ(n)); the amortization closes only because each mark pre-banks 2 potential units (the factor-2 in Φ=t+2m) to fund its eventual cascading cut — and marking's true purpose is to maintain the O(log n) degree bound that makes extract-min cheap, not to make decrease-key itself fast.**

# Stale-Read Root-Cause Analysis: `1-in-10⁴`, seconds-stale

## Reading the signature first (this constrains everything)

Three facts in the report do most of the discrimination work:

1. **Rate ≈ 1e-4.** This is a *narrow-window* signature. A systematic logic error (e.g. "the write path never invalidates the cache") would show up on a large fraction of read-after-write pairs, not 0.01%. A total outage (Redis down, replica broken) would be bursty and obvious. 1-in-10⁴ is the fingerprint of a **race condition** (a specific interleaving of concurrent read/write that only occasionally lines up) **or a rare transient** (a lag spike, a dropped message, a failed op that isn't retried). It effectively *rules out* the "always wrong" bugs.

2. **Staleness magnitude = "seconds."** There are only two clocks in this system that naturally tick in *seconds*: (a) **async replication lag** on the read-replica, and (b) a **TTL measured in seconds** governing how long a poisoned/uninvalidated cache entry survives. Sub-millisecond skew (single-node Redis primary propagation) is too small; hours-long staleness (a permanently poisoned entry under a long TTL) is too large. "Seconds" points squarely at replica lag or a short TTL persisting a bad entry.

3. **The fresh value provably existed and the read returned the old one.** This is *staleness*, not a *lost update* (write clobbered by a concurrent write) and not a *write failure*. So the write committed; the read path failed to observe it. That focuses attention on the read/populate path and the invalidation path, not on write atomicity.

Net: prioritize **races and transients on the cache-populate / invalidate path, with a "seconds" clock coming from replica lag or a short TTL.**

---

## Complete enumeration of plausible root causes

Grouped by mechanism. Each entry notes fit against `1e-4` + `seconds`.

### Group 1 — Read-through populate races (cache poisoned with a stale value)

**R1. Stale-set repopulation race (the classic "Facebook lease" bug).**
Interleaving: a reader gets a cache **miss** and reads value `v0` from the DB; *before it writes `v0` back*, a writer commits `v1` and **DELETEs** the key; then the slow reader's `SET key=v0` lands **after** the delete. Cache now holds `v0` and serves it until TTL or the next write. Requires the reader's DB-fetch to straddle the writer's commit+delete → naturally rare (**1e-4 fits**); persists for up to the TTL (**"seconds" fits if TTL is short**). This is the textbook cause and, given the exact signature, the leading hypothesis.

**R2. Same race, but the stale value comes from a lagging replica.**
Variant of R1 where the reader's populate reads the **async replica**, which is `v0` because it's seconds behind primary. Even without a delete race, a cache miss that reloads from a replica that hasn't replayed `v1` yet caches `v0`. Here the **"seconds" is literally the replication lag** — the cleanest possible explanation of the magnitude. Rare because it needs miss ∧ (routed to replica) ∧ (during the lag window).

**R3. Thundering-herd / stale-while-revalidate serving stale by design.**
Stampede-protection or soft-TTL logic deliberately returns the old value while a background refresh runs. Seconds-stale by construction; rare if it only triggers on contended keys.

### Group 2 — Invalidation-path defects (write commits, cache not correctly cleared)

**R4. Invalidate-before-commit ordering bug.**
Write path does `cache.DEL` **then** `db.commit()` (wrong order) instead of commit-then-invalidate. Any reader that misses in the gap reloads the *pre-commit* `v0` and repopulates; after commit the cache stays `v0`. This *widens* the R1 window dramatically. If present it tends to be more frequent than 1e-4 unless per-key write/read concurrency is low — worth checking precisely because it's a code-shape bug, not bad luck.

**R5. Missed / failed invalidation (fire-and-forget DEL).**
Writer commits, then the `DEL`/`SET` to Redis times out or errors and is **not retried**. Entry survives until TTL. Rate ≈ Redis-op failure rate (plausibly ~1e-4); staleness bounded by TTL (seconds if TTL is seconds; *this is the tell — if you see this cause, your TTL is short*).

**R6. Dropped cross-server invalidation message (only if per-instance caches exist).**
If there is an L1 / near-cache / HTTP-client cache in front of Redis and invalidation is broadcast via **Redis Pub/Sub**, delivery is **at-most-once, fire-and-forget** — under load a subscriber can miss the message and keep serving its local `v0` until the local TTL (seconds). Rate ≈ pub/sub drop rate. This is a *very* good fit for `1e-4` + seconds **if** any per-instance caching exists — flagged despite the "stateless" claim because "stateless" services frequently still memoize, and this is a commonly missed source. Requires validating the assumption.

**R7. Non-atomic dual-write reordering (write-through style).**
If the write path is "commit DB, then `SET cache=v1`," two concurrent writers can have their DB commits and their cache `SET`s land in opposite orders: DB ends `v1`, cache ends `v0`. Rare (needs concurrent writers to the same key), persists to TTL.

### Group 3 — Replica / storage-consistency

**R8. Plain replica-lag reads (no cache involvement).**
Reads that go straight to the replica (or cache miss → replica) see `v0` during the lag window. Overlaps R2; the "seconds" is the lag. Distinguished from R2 only by whether the stale value gets *cached* (persisting past the lag) or is transient (only during lag).

**R9. Replica lag *spikes* (checkpoint, vacuum, WAL replay stall, network).**
Baseline lag is sub-ms so read-your-writes usually works, but occasional spikes to seconds create the intermittent window → the 1e-4 could simply be "fraction of time lag > human-noticeable." Fits both axes well.

### Group 4 — Redis-internal / infra

**R10. Redis replica reads (Sentinel/Cluster with `READONLY`).**
If Redis is HA and the app reads from Redis **replicas**, the primary's `DEL`/`SET` propagates asynchronously; a replica can serve the old entry for a brief window. Usually milliseconds, so weaker fit for "seconds," unless Redis replication itself is lagging.

**R11. Redis failover losing recent invalidations.**
On failover, a promoted Redis replica that missed the last few `DEL`s resurfaces stale entries. Episodic/bursty, not steady 1e-4 — lower prior unless failovers are frequent.

**R12. maxmemory eviction → repopulate from lagging replica.**
Memory pressure evicts a key; the ensuing miss reloads from a lagging replica (→ R2). Compound, plausible under pressure.

### Group 5 — Edge / client

**R13. Intermediate HTTP caching (CDN / LB response cache / client cache).**
A short-TTL response cache at the LB/CDN serves a cached 200 for seconds. Fits both axes but is outside the store; only relevant if such a layer exists.

**R14. Clock skew driving premature/late TTL or version comparison.**
Skewed clocks across app servers cause a stale entry to be treated as fresh (or a versioned compare to pick the wrong one). Usually not "seconds"-consistent; lower prior.

**R15. Key collision / shard misroute.**
A small key subset hashes to the wrong node/old shard after a resize. Tends to be *systematic per key*, not uniformly 1e-4 across keys — lower prior, but cheap to exclude by checking whether stale reads cluster on specific keys/shards.

| Rank | Cause | Why the signature fits | Why not higher/lower |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1** | **R2 / R1 — read-through repopulation with a stale value (miss reloads `v0`, often from lagging replica, and caches it)** | Race → naturally ~1e-4; "seconds" = replica lag or short TTL; persists past the write exactly as observed | The single hypothesis that explains *both* the rarity and the magnitude without extra assumptions |
| **2** | **R8/R9 — replica-lag reads / lag spikes** | "Seconds" is the exact timescale of async lag; intermittency = lag-spike fraction | Slightly below #1 only if stale *persists* well past measured lag (that implies caching, i.e. R2) |
| **3** | **R5/R4 — missed or mis-ordered invalidation (failed DEL, or DEL-before-commit)** | Op-failure rate ~1e-4; stale bounded by (short) TTL | Ordering bug (R4) often *more* frequent than 1e-4; pure failed-DEL needs a short TTL to match "seconds" |
| 4 | R6 — dropped pub/sub invalidation to L1 caches | Excellent 1e-4+seconds fit **iff** per-instance caches exist | Gated on an assumption the topology says is false ("stateless") |
| 5 | R3 — stale-while-revalidate by design | Seconds-stale by construction | Only if such logic is deployed; usually intentional/known |
| 6 | R10/R12 — Redis replica reads / eviction+lag | Plausible but usually ms-scale | Weaker "seconds" fit unless Redis replication lags |
| 7 | R7/R11/R13/R14/R15 | Situational | Need specific preconditions; lower base rates |

**One-line rationale for the top cluster:** the only components with a *seconds* clock are the async replica and a short TTL, and the only thing that makes an error 1-in-10⁴ instead of constant is a race or a transient — the intersection is "a rare cache-populate that captures a not-yet-replicated value (or races a delete) and pins it in cache for a short TTL."

## Definitive tests for the top 3 (each isolates one cause from the others)

These are designed as a **discriminating ladder** — run them in order; each one, by construction, is negative for the other two causes.

### Test for #1 — Repopulation race (R1/R2): *prove a reader SET landed after the writer's DEL, with a pre-commit read*

**Instrument, don't guess.** Store the value in Redis as `(value, db_version)` where `db_version` is a monotonic write counter or the row's `xmin`/`updated_at` (nanoseconds). Then:

- **Passive detector (definitive log):** on every Redis write, log `(key, db_version, source, t_dbread, t_set)` where `source ∈ {writer, reader-repopulate}`; on every writer invalidation log `(key, t_commit, t_del)`. A confirmed R1/R2 event has the exact temporal fingerprint:
  `t_dbread(reader) < t_commit(writer) < t_del(writer) < t_set(reader)` **and** the cached `db_version` is *older* than the committed one. No other cause produces a reader-sourced SET that is newer than the writer's DEL yet carries an older version. Seeing even one such record is proof.

- **Active confirmation (kill switch):** enable **stale-set prevention** on one canary app server only — populate with `SET key val NX` (or a lease/CAS token: only write back if the key is still absent / the lease is still valid). Route this canary's cache-miss reloads to the **primary** (so replica lag can't be the cause on the canary). If stale reads for keys served by the canary drop to ~0 while the fleet's rate is unchanged → the repopulation race is confirmed and is the cause. (Reading primary here is what separates this from Test #2.)

**Distinguishes from #2/#3:** replica lag can't create a *version-inverted, post-DEL* SET; a failed/mis-ordered DEL leaves the *writer's* stale value, not a *reader-repopulated* one.

### Test for #2 — Replica lag (R8/R9): *correlate stale events with measured lag, then remove the replica from the read path*

- **Metric correlation (definitive):** tag every cache-*populating* DB read with the backend it hit (`primary` vs `replica`) and, for replica reads, the replica's lag at fetch time via `EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (now() - pg_last_xact_replay_timestamp()))` (or `pg_stat_replication.replay_lag` on the primary). Then test two predictions that *only* replica lag makes:
  1. **Every** stale read's populate was sourced from the **replica** (never primary), and
  2. the measured **staleness ≈ the replica lag at that instant**, and the **rate of stale reads rises and falls with lag spikes** (overlay the two time series; they should be near-coincident).

- **Active confirmation (kill switch):** temporarily route **all cache-miss reloads to the primary** (or require read-your-writes routing / `synchronous_commit=on` for the affected reads). If stale reads vanish → replica lag confirmed. If they persist → it is *not* replica lag (push to Test #1 or #3).

**Distinguishes from #1/#3:** primary-only reloads eliminate lag but do **not** fix a delete-race (#1) or a failed/mis-ordered invalidation (#3) — those persist because they concern the *cache write/invalidate* path, not which DB replica was read.

### Test for #3 — Missed / mis-ordered invalidation (R5/R4): *make the writer's DEL post-commit, guaranteed, and confirmed — see if the rate collapses*

- **Metric (definitive log):** instrument the write path to emit, per write, `(key, t_commit, del_issued_before_or_after_commit, del_result ∈ {ok, error, timeout}, del_retries)`. Two direct reads:
  - If a measurable fraction (~1e-4) of writes log `del_result ≠ ok` **and those exact keys are the ones later read stale**, that is a confirmed **missed invalidation (R5)**.
  - If `del_issued_before_commit = true` anywhere, you have the **ordering bug (R4)** in code — and the stale keys will correlate with reads that missed during the pre-commit gap.

- **Active confirmation (kill switch):** deploy a write path that is **commit → then DEL, retried until acknowledged** (durable invalidation: outbox/txn-log-driven delete, or synchronous confirmed DEL with retry). This makes the writer's invalidation *bulletproof and correctly ordered* without touching the reader path or the replica.
  - If the stale rate collapses → it was **#3**.
  - If stale reads **still occur** with a bulletproof, correctly-ordered, always-acknowledged single DEL → invalidation is not the culprit; by elimination it is the **reader repopulation race (#1)** or **replica lag (#2)**. This is precisely the experiment that separates #3 from #1: #1 survives a perfect DEL (because the offending SET comes from a *concurrent reader after* the DEL), whereas #3 does not.

**Distinguishes from #1/#2:** a guaranteed post-commit DEL fixes only writer-side invalidation defects; it leaves both the reader-repopulation race and replica lag untouched.

### Decision tree (fastest path to a verdict)

1. Route cache-miss reloads to **primary**. Fixed? → **replica lag (#2)**. Else →
2. Make writer DEL **post-commit + retried + acknowledged**. Fixed? → **missed/mis-ordered invalidation (#3)**. Else →
3. Add **NX/lease stale-set prevention** on populate. Fixed? → **repopulation race (#1)**.

Each step is negative-by-construction for the other two, so the first step that stops the bleeding names the cause unambiguously. Run the passive instrumentation (versioned cache entries + populate-source + DEL-outcome logs) in parallel from the start — in most cases the logs alone identify the culprit before you need the kill switches, because the `read < commit < del < set` version-inverted record (for #1), the lag/stale time-series coincidence (for #2), and the failed-DEL-to-stale-key correlation (for #3) are mutually exclusive fingerprints.

**Assumption to verify before all of the above:** confirm whether any **per-instance L1/near-cache or HTTP-client cache** exists in the "stateless" app servers. If it does, promote **R6 (dropped Pub/Sub invalidation)** to the top tier and add a fourth test — sequence-number every invalidation message and have each subscriber log gaps; a missing sequence number on a server that then serves stale is definitive for R6. The topology as stated says Redis is the only cache, but this is the highest-value assumption to falsify because it would reorder the whole ranking.

# Stale-Read Root-Cause Analysis: clients → LB → app servers → Redis (read-through) → Postgres primary + async replica

## 0. First, decode the signature

Two numbers carry almost all the diagnostic information:

**"1 in 10,000" (P ≈ 10⁻⁴)** — this is a *coincidence rate*, i.e. the product of two modest probabilities, or a small per-operation failure rate. It is:
- Too **low** to be a misconfigured server (1 bad server out of N gives P ≈ 1/N ≈ 10⁻¹–10⁻²), a systematically wrong read path, or "TTL-only, no invalidation" design (that scales with write rate and would be far noisier on hot keys).
- Too **high and too steady** to be failover/split-brain events (those are bursty: zero for weeks, then thousands of stale reads in one minute).
- Exactly right for `P(cache miss) × P(key was written within window W before the miss)`. Example: 2% miss rate × (1s window / 60s mean inter-write interval on read keys) ≈ 3×10⁻⁴.

**"Seconds stale"** — the staleness magnitude names the mechanism's clock:
- **Seconds** is the natural timescale of: Postgres **async replica lag** under load, **short cache TTLs**, **async invalidation pipelines** (pub/sub, CDC, queues), leaked-transaction MVCC snapshots, and tail GC/network pauses widening race windows.
- It is *not* the natural timescale of: healthy intra-DC Redis replication (sub-ms–ms), DNS TTLs (minutes), long cache TTLs (minutes–hours), or crash-recovery data loss (permanent).

**One subtlety that matters for the whole analysis (amplification):** in a read-through architecture, any mechanism that gets a stale value *into* Redis converts one rare poisoning event into `read_rate_on_key × min(TTL, time-to-next-invalidation)` stale reads. So the observed 10⁻⁴ read-level rate may be produced by a poisoning-event rate that is 10–1000× rarer. When ranking causes, think in terms of *poisoning events*, not stale reads.

Also verify the observation itself before debugging: "overwritten seconds earlier" is usually established by comparing a write log timestamp against a read log timestamp — **clock skew between hosts can manufacture phantom staleness**. Cheap check: a canary key written with a monotonic counter every second by one writer, read continuously, with both operations logged through the same clock. If the canary never shows staleness, keep it running — it becomes your detector for every experiment below.

## 1. Full enumeration of plausible root causes

### Tier A — strong signature fit (both rate and timescale match)

**A1. Cache-miss repopulation sourced from the async replica.**
On a miss, the read-through loader's SELECT lands on the replica (deliberately "for read scaling," or accidentally via pgbouncer/HAProxy/RDS-proxy pool mixing, a DNS name that round-robins primary+replica, a reader-endpoint DSN in the cache-fill code path, or a subset of pooled connections pinned to the replica). Writes go to the primary and invalidate Redis; a miss within the lag window re-caches the pre-write value.
*Fit:* staleness = replica lag = seconds, exactly. Rate = miss% × P(recent write) ≈ 10⁻⁴. **Best single fit.**

**A2. Cache-aside / read-through repopulation race ("stale SET after invalidate").**
Classic interleaving: reader misses → reads DB (old value) → is delayed (GC pause, network hiccup, slow event loop) → meanwhile writer commits new value and DELETEs the key → delayed reader SETs the *old* value. The poisoned entry then serves stale reads for seconds (until TTL or the next write).
*Fit:* poisoning rate = miss% × (DB-fetch latency / inter-write interval) ≈ 10⁻⁵–10⁻⁶, amplified by reads-per-key-per-TTL back up to ~10⁻⁴. "Seconds stale" = short TTL or next invalidation. Includes the single-flight/dogpile-lock variant (a fetch that *started* before the write commits *after* the invalidation) and the write-side ordering variant (invalidate-then-write-DB, reader repopulates in between).

**A3. Failed, dropped, or asynchronous cache invalidation.**
The DELETE after a write is fire-and-forget and occasionally times out / errors / is swallowed by an exception handler; or invalidation rides an async channel (Redis pub/sub — which is at-most-once, keyspace notifications, CDC/Debezium, a queue) that delays or loses messages. Stale value survives until TTL.
*Fit:* rate = per-write invalidation-failure rate (10⁻³–10⁻⁵ is typical for timeouts under load) × read amplification; "seconds" fits if TTL is short or the async channel's delay is seconds.

### Tier B — plausible, fits one axis well, check after Tier A

**B1. Stale MVCC snapshot on a pooled Postgres connection.** A connection returned to the pool while *idle in transaction* (leaked ORM session, missing commit/rollback on an error path, `REPEATABLE READ` default) — the next borrower reads a snapshot taken seconds ago. Rate = fraction of requests that draw the poisoned connection; staleness = age of the leaked transaction. Detectable via `pg_stat_activity` (`state = 'idle in transaction'`, old `xact_start`).

**B2. Hidden in-process cache on the "stateless" app servers.** An ORM second-level cache, `lru_cache`/caffeine/Guava memoizer with a seconds-TTL, a request-scoped cache leaking across requests, or a module-level variable. Server A serves its local copy after server B wrote. "Seconds stale" matches a seconds TTL exactly; rate = P(local hit on a recently-overwritten key).

**B3. Redis-side topology staleness.** Reading from Redis replicas (`READONLY` in cluster mode, replica reads enabled in the client), Sentinel failover with lost acked writes, or two app servers holding *different shard maps* during a config rollout (write/invalidate goes to shard A, read hits shard B's old copy). Healthy intra-DC Redis lag is ms not seconds (weakens the fit), and failover/rollout causes are bursty rather than steady 10⁻⁴ — rank below Tier A unless you run cross-region Redis replication (ElastiCache Global Datastore etc.), which *does* have seconds of lag and would jump to Tier A.

**B4. HTTP-layer caching above the app servers.** LB/CDN/proxy or client honoring a leaked `Cache-Control: max-age=…`/ETag on a few endpoints, caching GETs for seconds. Rate = fraction of traffic hitting a warm proxy entry. Trivially checkable: stale responses that never appear in app-server access logs.

### Tier C — possible but signature-mismatched; rule out cheaply

- **C1. Delayed duplicate write replay** (queue retry / at-least-once consumer / LB retry of a non-idempotent POST re-applies the *old* value after the new one). Distinguishing fingerprint: the *database itself* holds the old value afterward — it's not a stale read, it's a real regression of state.
- **C2. Last-write-wins with clock skew** dropping the newer write (only if the write path uses timestamps for conflict resolution — unusual in this stack; same DB-holds-old-value fingerprint as C1).
- **C3. Write-behind / async DB persistence**: cache updated, DB write deferred; a concurrent miss reads the not-yet-written DB. Only if such a component exists.
- **C4. One misconfigured app server** (wrong Redis endpoint, replica DSN for all reads). Rate would be ~1/N ≈ 10⁻¹–10⁻², 2–3 orders too high — ruled out *as a sole cause*, but "one server × only cache-miss paths" can land at 10⁻⁴, so keep it as a sub-hypothesis of A1 (check per-server stale-rate skew).
- **C5. Redis eviction pressure (`maxmemory`)** — not a root cause itself, but raises miss rate and therefore multiplies A1/A2.
- **C6. Monitoring artifact / clock skew in logs** — see §0; rule out first, it costs an hour.

## 3. Definitive tests for the top 3

### Test 1 — A1 (cache fill reads the replica)

**Dose–response experiment (the smoking gun):** in a canary/staging environment — or briefly in production during low traffic — run `SELECT pg_wal_replay_pause();` on the replica for 60 s, then `pg_wal_replay_resume();`. If A1 is the cause, the stale-read rate **rises during the pause and the measured staleness grows linearly to ~60 s**, tracking the induced lag exactly. No other cause on the list responds to replica replay state: A2's race window is set by app fetch latency, A3's by TTL/invalidation delivery — both are indifferent to the replica.
**Non-invasive confirmations:** (a) on the replica, enable `log_statement`/`pg_stat_statements` and look for the cache-fill SELECTs — *any* occurrence on the replica of a query that should feed Redis is proof of the routing defect; also `pg_stat_activity` on the replica for app-server client addresses. (b) Plot stale-event count vs. `now() - pg_last_xact_replay_timestamp()` (or `pg_stat_replication.replay_lag` on the primary) — A1 predicts stale events concentrate in high-lag minutes and per-event staleness ≤ concurrent lag.
**Fix-confirms:** point the cache-fill DSN at the primary for 24 h; A1 predicts stale reads drop to ~zero, and per-server breakdown identifies a C4 variant (one server's rate ≫ others).

### Test 2 — A2 (invalidate/repopulate race)

**Instrumentation fingerprint:** embed a monotonic version (`updated_at` or a version column) inside every cached value, and log every cache `SET k` with `(version, t_db_read_start, t_set)` and every `DEL k` with timestamp. A2 has a unique, unambiguous log signature: **a `SET(k, version=v_old)` whose `t_db_read_start` precedes a `DEL(k)` for the same key, with `t_set` after it.** Neither A1 (the SET carries a *replica-stale* version but with no interleaved DEL between read-start and set) nor A3 (no SET involved at all — the DEL simply never landed) produces this interleaving. With versions in the cache you can also audit live: sample keys and compare Redis version vs. primary version.
**Amplification experiment (dose–response):** in a canary, inject an artificial 200 ms sleep between the DB fetch and the cache SET in the read-through loader. A2 predicts the stale rate on that canary rises by roughly `200ms / normal_fetch_latency` (1–2 orders of magnitude); A1 and A3 predict no change. Conversely, deploying a compare-and-swap SET (Lua: set only if embedded version is newer than the resident one) or a post-invalidation tombstone window should drive the rate to zero *only* if A2 is the cause.

### Test 3 — A3 (failed / async invalidation)

**Write-side verification probe:** after every DB write, schedule an async check at +100 ms and +2 s that reads the Redis key and asserts it is either absent or carries the new version, logging violations *with the causal classification*:
- key **never deleted** (no DEL logged / DEL returned error or timed out) → **A3 confirmed**, and the client-side DEL error counter (plus Redis `SLOWLOG` and timeout metrics at the same instants) tells you which failure mode;
- key **was deleted, then reappeared with the old version** → that is A2, not A3 (the probe cleanly separates the two, which naive "cache is stale" checks cannot);
- key holds an old version **and the DEL succeeded and nothing re-set it** per logs → look upstream (async invalidation channel). For pub/sub–based invalidation, compare published vs. received invalidation counts per app server — Redis pub/sub is at-most-once, so any gap under connection churn is the answer; the stale-read rate will correlate with subscriber reconnect events.
**Static tell:** grep the write path for fire-and-forget deletes (no await/no error handling). If invalidation delay rather than loss is suspected, measure publish→delivery latency with a heartbeat invalidation message; A3-by-delay predicts staleness duration ≈ that latency distribution.

DELIVERABLE: a ranked hypothesis set with differential diagnostics. No single cause is asserted as THE answer; the ranking is gated by five topology facts you must read from config/code first, because they make several causes physically possible or impossible.

== WHAT THE SIGNATURE ACTUALLY CONSTRAINS (stated carefully) ==
- Rate ~1e-4. The tempting shortcut "1e-4 => a narrow race, not a misconfiguration" is WRONG and I deliberately do not lead with it (all three source attempts overreached here and were independently refuted on exactly this point). An async replica serving reads with a perfectly normal small lag L ALSO produces a rare stale rate: a read is stale only if its key was written within the last ~L seconds AND the read landed on the lagging path. Over a large keyspace that temporal coincidence is naturally ~1e-4, with no misconfiguration and no sub-millisecond window. So 1e-4 is consistent with BOTH a narrow reorder race AND a routine replica-read path. What 1e-4 DOES exclude is gross persistent per-key breakage (a key that is never invalidated would make ~100% of its reads stale), not systematic routing.
- "Overwritten seconds earlier." The wrong value's age is a few seconds. This excludes a sub-ms hiccup and points either at a component genuinely seconds behind (replication catch-up) or a cache entry that lives ~seconds (short TTL / cleared by the next write on a hot key).
- Self-heals (this is an INFERENCE from "intermittent," not stated in the task - flagged). If the value later corrects on its own, that excludes durable corruption (a bad commit; cache poisoning that outlives a long TTL) and admits only transient-catch-up or TTL/next-write-bounded mechanisms.

The most useful lever from this is the CORRECTION-TIME DISTRIBUTION: does staleness heal at a variable horizon that tracks a replication-lag gauge (points to lag on a directly-served replica read), or at a horizon pinned to a fixed TTL / the next write (points to a poisoned cache entry)? Caveat: under a read-through cache, replica lag on the POPULATE path writes the stale value INTO Redis, so it then persists until TTL/next-write like a race - "correction tracks the lag gauge" only holds for a DIRECTLY replica-served (uncached) read path, not the populate path. (Attempt 1's version of this test ignored that and was correctly flagged.)

== FERMI RECONCILIATION (corrected) ==
Do not use the dimensionally-broken formula stale_fraction ~ (W*L)/R (writes/s * seconds / reads/s has units of seconds, not a probability). The correct stale probability for a lag/race mechanism is per-key: P(stale read of key k) ~ (per-key write rate of k) * L, then averaged over the read distribution. Consequence: the achievable rate depends on keyspace cardinality and hot-key write recency, so 1e-4 does NOT by itself pin race-vs-lag-vs-lossy-channel. Two anchors: (a) a ~few-ms populate-reorder window on hot keys written ~1/s gives ~1e-3 for THOSE keys, diluted across mostly-cold traffic to ~1e-4; (b) a fire-and-forget invalidation dropping ~1e-4 of messages gives ~1e-4 directly. Both fit; the arithmetic discriminates only against always-100% per-key breakage.

== FIVE TOPOLOGY GATES TO CONFIRM FIRST (each reshuffles the rank) ==
G1. Do cache MISSES (or any read path - ORM read/write split, reporting endpoints) hit the Postgres PRIMARY only, or the async REPLICA? The diagram routes read-through to the primary, which demotes Postgres replica lag UNLESS a hidden replica read path exists.
G2. Write-side cache action: synchronous DEL/invalidate, write-through, or TTL-only? And does it fire BEFORE or AFTER commit? The populate race and the write-ordering bug only exist under invalidate-based coherence.
G3. Is there an L1 in-process/per-node cache in front of Redis? If yes, LB routing yields per-node seconds-staleness that is INVISIBLE in Redis and Postgres metrics.
G4. Is Redis single-node, or master/replica with reads served from replicas (client READONLY / replica endpoints)? Redis replica lag reproduces the whole signature and is invisible in Postgres metrics.
G5. What is the Redis (and any L1) TTL - seconds or minutes? If minutes, the lost-invalidation and L1 causes would produce minutes-scale staleness, contradicting "seconds," and get demoted.

== FULL CAUSE TAXONOMY (exhaustive for this stack) ==
A. Read-through populate / stale-set race: a reader misses, loads V_old from the DB, and SETs it into Redis just AFTER a concurrent writer's DEL(K) for V_new. Cache holds V_old until next write or TTL. (The Facebook-memcache "stale set," fixed there with leases / single-flight fills.)
B. Postgres async replica-lag read: a read/populate served from the lagging replica returns V_old. Gated by G1.
C. Redis async replication read: a read served by a Redis replica behind the master (SET/DEL not yet propagated). Gated by G4. Same signature as B, different layer, invisible in Postgres metrics.
D. Lost/dropped invalidation on a lossy channel (pub/sub, keyspace notifications, async queue, occasionally-failing DEL): ~1e-4 of invalidations dropped, cache holds V_old until TTL. Gated by G5.
E. L1 per-node in-process cache + LB routing: node-local cache with its own TTL serves stale; invisible in Redis/PG metrics. Gated by G3.
F. Write-side ordering bug: invalidate-before-commit (a concurrent reader repopulates the pre-commit value) or cache-then-DB. A structural variant of A.
G. Non-atomic check-then-set / TTL-boundary race: concurrent fillers after expiry, last-writer stores an older computed value.
H. Long-lived transaction snapshot: a pooled connection holding a REPEATABLE READ / stale MVCC snapshot returns an already-overwritten value; heals when the transaction ends.
I. Clock skew across nodes affecting TTL expiry or timestamp-based last-write-wins.
J. Write-retry replay (at-least-once / idempotency bug): a retried write re-applies an old payload after V_new landed; heals at next write.
K. Client-side / CDN / HTTP caching at the "clients" tier (Cache-Control, browser or edge cache) - a layer above the LB the named components never see. (Included so the enumeration covers the whole path.)

== RANKING (by joint match to rate AND seconds/self-heal, gates applied) ==
1 (co-lead). A - Read-through populate/stale-set race. Gate-independent (operates on Redis, the actual serving layer), always possible under G2=invalidate, native signature matches all three features: rarity = the ms-scale fill window, horizon = until next write/TTL (seconds on hot keys), heals at next write. Highest prior for this topology.
2 (co-lead, gated). Replication lag serving stale reads - Redis replica (C, if G4 enables replica reads) OR Postgres replica (B, only via a hidden read path per G1). The cleanest literal match to "seconds-stale, self-heals" (catch-up horizon). Held at co-lead, not sole #1, precisely because it requires a replica read path.
3. D - Lost invalidation on a lossy channel. Rate = drop probability (~1e-4 plausible for fire-and-forget pub/sub); horizon = up to TTL, heals at the TTL boundary. Fits cleanly IF TTL ~ seconds (G5).
Below: F (write-ordering, wider-window variant of A) > E (L1 wildcard - promote into top 3 if G3 confirms an L1 cache, since it is invisible everywhere else) > G (CAS/TTL race) > H (transaction snapshot; usually >1e-4 only with genuinely long transactions) > K (client/CDN cache; check Cache-Control) > J (retry replay) > I (clock skew; needs timestamp-LWW logic).
Explicitly demoted: any persistent "this key never invalidates" bug (would be ~100%, not 1e-4) and any cold-key corruption that would outlast "seconds."

== SHARED INSTRUMENT (one build, powers all three tests) ==
Store a monotonic VERSION with each cached value (Postgres commit LSN, xmin, or a write sequence number). Tag every served read with: {hit|miss, redis_node=master|replica-id, db_backend=primary|replica-id, served_version, source_version_at_fill, cache_populated_at, cache_last_del_at, app_node_id}. Log every SET and DEL with {key, wall-clock, version}. At a detected stale read, compare served_version vs latest_committed_version and dump the key's recent op history.

== TOP-3 DEFINITIVE, DIFFERENTIAL TESTS ==

TEST 1 - isolates the POPULATE RACE (A) and distinguishes it from replica-lag masquerade. The naive version (look for DEL(v2) then SET(v1<v2)) is NOT sufficient: a cache miss that repopulates from a LAGGING replica after a primary-side invalidation produces the SAME DEL(v2)-then-SET(v1) ordering (this is the flaw that got Attempt 2 refuted). The FIX grafts Attempt 1's backend/source tag onto Attempt 2's op-log: require DEL(v2)-then-SET(v1) AND fill source_backend = PRIMARY AND source_version_at_fill was already >= v2 at the fill's read timestamp - i.e. the source was FRESH and only the timing reordered. Mapping: (fresh-source, primary, reordered) => true populate race A; (source_backend=replica with source_version < v2 at read time) => this was replica lag B/C, NOT the race. Intervention confirmation: enable a Redis lease / single-flight fill on hot keys (the memcache fix); if the stale rate collapses, A confirmed.

TEST 2 - isolates REPLICATION LAG (B or C) via a point-away experiment (the strongest single differential; survives in all three attempts). Passive: stale reads should carry served-by = a specific replica (Redis replica-id or PG replica) whose replay-lag gauge >= the observed staleness, and should NEVER appear on master/primary-served reads. Definitive: stand up a CANARY app fleet pinned to Redis-master-only + Postgres-primary-only reads. If stale reads VANISH on the canary => replication lag (identify PG-vs-Redis by which backend tag the baseline stale reads carried). If they PERSIST on primary/master-only => lag falsified, because A, D, F all occur even when everything is served by master/primary. This beats "just read the lag gauge," which proves lag EXISTS but not that the stale value was SERVED by the laggard.

TEST 3 - isolates LOST INVALIDATION (D). Sequence-number every invalidation publish and ACK; expose invalidations_published vs invalidations_applied counters, and store the last-applied invalidation-seq beside each value. Correlate stale-read events with the condition "a write committed for this key but NO DEL was observed in the interval." Distinguishing shape: a persistent cache HIT with NO preceding DEL, entry.invalidation-seq < last-write seq, correction pinned near the TTL ceiling; and stale_rate == measured (published - applied) drop rate. Contrast: A shows a DEL PRESENT then an older SET (Test 1); B/C show a replica-served, transient correction near catch-up with no poisoned entry (Test 2). Intervention confirmation: replace the lossy channel with a synchronous DEL (or shorten TTL and watch max staleness track it exactly - A and B/C do not respond to TTL); if stale reads vanish, D confirmed.

Each test yields DIFFERENT observations under the rivals (fill-backend primary-vs-replica and fresh-vs-stale-at-read; DEL present-vs-absent; correction at-next-write vs tracking-lag vs pinned-at-TTL; stale reads vanish-vs-persist under master/primary pinning), so each rules a cause IN or OUT rather than merely being consistent with it. Confirm G1-G5 first: they can promote C or E into the top 3, or demote B out of it.
