# Hot-counter under high write contention: analytical trade-off and an outage-correct policy

## 0. What actually limits a "counter"

An increment is a **read-modify-write on one logical location**. Under concurrency that location must be serialized somewhere, so throughput is bounded by the rate at which the serialization point can retire one increment:

```
Throughput_ceiling ≈ 1 / T_crit
```

where `T_crit` is the effective critical-section time (lock hold + whatever must happen durably/coherently before the next writer can proceed). **The entire comparison reduces to (i) how big `T_crit` is per backend, and (ii) how many independent serialization points you can create.**

The right load variable is **concurrency `C`** (number of simultaneously in-flight increments), not raw rate `λ`. By Little's law `C = λ · T_service`. Contention scales with `C`.

A useful frame is the Universal Scalability Law:
```
Speedup(N) = N / (1 + α(N−1) + βN(N−1))
```
- `α` = serialization fraction, `β` = cross-talk/coherence cost.
- A **single hot location has α ≈ 1** → no parallel section → flat ceiling; and with `β > 0` (lock convoy, cache-line bouncing, MVCC bloat) throughput **retrogrades** (goes *down*) as `C` grows. That retrograde behavior — not just a plateau — is the thing sharding exists to kill.

---

## 1. (a) Postgres single-row `UPDATE t SET n=n+1 WHERE id=k`

**Mechanics / why `T_crit` is large.** Writers to the same row strictly serialize: an `UPDATE` locks the tuple (`xmax`), and a second writer must **wait for the first transaction to commit or abort** before it can even produce its new row version. Each transaction on the critical path must, with `synchronous_commit=on`, **fsync the WAL** before releasing. So:

```
T_crit(pg-1row) ≈ lock + new-tuple + WAL fsync + commit
              ≈ 0.5 – 2 ms on SSD  →  ceiling ≈ 500 – 2000 incr/s
```

**Group commit does not help here.** Group/batched commit amortizes fsync across *different* concurrent transactions. Same-row writers **cannot overlap their critical sections at all**, so they cannot be batched — the second cannot start modifying until the first commits. This is exactly the α≈1 case.

**Retrograde (β) sources as `C` grows:**
- **Lock convoy:** `C` writers queue on the tuple lock → per-request latency ≈ `C · T_crit` (p99 explodes linearly) while throughput stays flat.
- **MVCC bloat:** each increment makes a dead tuple. HOT updates mitigate *only if* the counter column is unindexed and the page has fillfactor headroom; at high rate autovacuum falls behind → page/index bloat → `T_crit` grows → actual retrograde throughput.

**Read accuracy:** **Exact and strongly consistent, durable.** A read is one index lookup returning the last committed value. This is (a)'s whole selling point.

**Verdict:** unbeatable simplicity and correctness; throughput ceiling ~10²–10³/s (sync commit), maybe ~10⁴/s with `synchronous_commit=off`/batching at the cost of a durability window. Falls over in the 10³–10⁴ band.

---

## 2. (b) Redis `INCR`

**Why `T_crit` is ~1000× smaller.** Classic Redis is a **single-threaded event loop**; `INCR` is an in-memory integer add, atomic by virtue of the single thread — no lock, no fsync in the request path (AOF `everysec`/RDB flush off the hot path).

```
T_crit(redis) ≈ in-memory add ≈ 1–10 µs (exec)
ceiling(single key) ≈ 10^5 incr/s (request/reply)
                    ≈ 10^6 incr/s (pipelined / locally batched)
```

Redis wins purely because its critical section is ~1000× shorter than a durable Postgres commit. Same serialization, tiny cost.

**Two real limits:**
- **One core per hot key.** Serialization is inherent in the event loop; you **cannot** scale a *single* key across cores/nodes by cluster sharding, because the key hashes to one slot/node. Beyond the single-core ceiling you must shard the key (→ option c) or aggregate in the app.
- **Network RTT** dominates *unpipelined* remote calls; N app servers doing synchronous `INCR` are bounded by `connections / RTT`. Local aggregation / pipelining is what unlocks the high numbers.

**Read accuracy — the trap.** Live reads are exact w.r.t. what the instance has applied, **but durability/failover is weak**:
- Crash loses the **unsynced window** = `λ · fsync_interval` (AOF `everysec` → up to ~1 s of increments; RDB → up to the snapshot interval).
- **Async replication** → failover to a replica silently drops the tail of increments (lost writes / split-brain).

This loss is **permanent and one-directional**, unlike the transient skew of option (c). **Therefore Redis cannot be the system of record for a count you must not lose.**

---

## 3. (c) Sharded / approximate counter (N sub-counters summed on read)

**Idea:** split into N shards; each increment hits one shard (random, or keyed by server/thread id); read = sum of N shards. Applies to *both* backends:
- **PG-sharded:** N rows → up to N independent tuple locks → up to N× the single-row ceiling until the instance's global WAL/IO/CPU commit ceiling (~10⁴–10⁵ durable commits/s). Read = `SELECT sum(n) FROM shards WHERE counter=k`.
- **Redis-sharded:** N keys spread across slots/nodes → spreads across cores until client/network limit.

**Throughput model (balls-in-bins).** With `C` concurrent writers and N shards, expected writers per shard ≈ `C/N`, so per-shard contention drops ~linearly:
```
Throughput_sharded(N) ≈ min( N · (1/T_crit_single) , Global_ceiling )
```
Pick **N on the order of the peak concurrent-writer count** (`N ≳ C`) so per-shard contention → ~1. Beyond that, **diminishing returns**: you've hit the global IO/CPU ceiling, more shards add no throughput but *do* add read cost and storage → there is an optimal N (typically 32–256 for a single PG instance).

**Read accuracy — where "approximate" comes from.** The sum over N shards is **not necessarily atomic**:
- **PG:** a single-statement `SELECT sum(...)` runs under **one MVCC snapshot** → the aggregate is **point-in-time exact** (consistent as of the snapshot instant). PG-sharded reads stay *exact*.
- **Redis:** reading N keys needs `MGET`/N `GET`s. `MGET` on **one node is atomic**, but **cross-slot (multi-node) is not** → shard 1 may be read before an increment and shard 5 after it → skew. This is the "approximate" in approximate counters — you trade atomic exactness for spread.

**Magnitude of the skew error.** Model increments as Poisson `λ`; a read spanning `δ` seconds can tear only the in-flight writes:
```
E|ε_skew| = O(λ · δ)      (transient, self-correcting: exact once writes quiesce)
relative error = λδ / total → 0 as the count grows
```
So a sharded like-count gets **relatively more accurate as it gets large** — a good property. Contrast with Redis durability loss `λ · fsync_interval`, which is **permanent**. (There is a *different* "approximate" — Morris/HyperLogLog probabilistic counters that trade **accuracy for memory**, relative error a fixed %; not what's needed for a like-count, but worth distinguishing.)

**Cost of reads scales with N** → if reads ≫ writes, maintain a rolled-up materialized value rather than summing N every read.

---

## 4. Crossover points (order-of-magnitude; assumptions in §6)

| Offered load `λ` | Recommended | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `λ ≲ 10³/s` | **(a) PG single row** | Below the single-row commit ceiling. Exact + durable + simplest. No reason to add Redis or shard. |
| `10³ – 10⁵/s` | **(c) PG-sharded** (N ≈ #concurrent writers) *or* **(b) Redis** | PG single row saturates and goes retrograde (bloat + convoy). PG-sharded multiplies the ceiling by N and **stays exact+durable**. Redis handles it on one key if you accept a rebuildable cache + lower latency. This is the main crossover band. |
| `10⁵ – 10⁶/s` | **(b) Redis `INCR`, single key**, backed by a durable ledger | Above the single-instance PG commit ceiling even sharded (~10⁴–10⁵ durable commits/s). Redis single-core handles this. |
| `λ ≳ 10⁶/s` | **App-tier local aggregation** (= sharding taken to the app: shard = server) + periodic flush | Even Redis's single event loop saturates on one key. Each server keeps a local counter, flushes deltas every T. Store sees only `#servers / T` writes; per-increment cost decouples from the network entirely. Reads become eventually-consistent with lag ~T. |

**The two crossovers with closed forms:**
- **(a)→(c/pg) or (b):** at `λ ≈ 1/T_crit(pg-1row)` ≈ a few hundred–few thousand/s (sync commit).
- **(b single key)→(c sharded/app):** at `λ ≈ single-core Redis ceiling` ≈ 10⁵–10⁶/s.

---

## 5. Policy that is correct under a Redis outage

**Define "correct" for a like-count:** monotonic (never visibly decreases), **no lost acknowledged increments**, write-available during a Redis outage (don't drop likes), and eventually exact.

Redis alone violates durability (async replication + fsync window) → **Redis must never be the system of record.** Recommended architecture: **treat every fast counter as a rebuildable projection of a durable, idempotent source of truth.**

**Exploit the like-count's structure.** A like-count is `COUNT(DISTINCT user)` over likes, so the source of truth is a **set, not a mutable integer**:

1. **Durable, idempotent ingest (never lose a like):** `INSERT INTO likes(user_id, item_id) ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`, PK `(user_id, item_id)`.
   - **Appends go to different tuples/pages → no hot-row contention** (this is why an append-only ledger scales orders of magnitude better than `UPDATE` of one row).
   - The PK makes it **naturally deduped/idempotent** → safe under at-least-once retries and Redis failover (at-least-once + non-idempotent `INCR` = overcount; the PK removes that hazard).

2. **Fast read path (derived):** on a *new* insert, `INCRBY` a Redis counter (and/or maintain a PG sharded rollup). Redis is a **cache rebuildable from `likes`**.

3. **Redis outage behavior:**
   - **Writes: unaffected** — they still insert into `likes`. Make the write-through to Redis **non-fatal** (log-and-continue). No likes lost.
   - **Reads: fall back** to the PG rollup (sharded-sum) value, optionally + count of unprocessed rows. Reads stay available, monotonic, correct-up-to-lag.
   - **Recovery: rebuild** `SET key = <authoritative rollup/COUNT>` then resume `INCRBY` from the ledger offset. **Idempotent replay via the like PK / ledger offset → exactly-once fold**, no double count.

4. **Published SLA:** Redis-served reads are near-real-time; during an outage, PG-served reads lag by the rollup interval. The count is **eventually exact** because `likes` is complete.

**Net:** a Redis outage degrades **read latency/freshness, not correctness.** Both the Redis `INCR` and any PG hot row are *derived, rebuildable, fast-read projections*; the durable idempotent set is authoritative.

If you don't have a natural idempotency key (a generic counter, not likes), substitute an **append-only increment ledger** (PG `events` table or Kafka) carrying a unique increment id; a consumer folds it into Redis/PG-rollup with dedup by id. Same properties.

---

## 6. Assumptions (make the numbers honest)

- **PG numbers** assume `synchronous_commit=on`, SSD fsync ~0.2–1 ms, single primary. `synchronous_commit=off`/batched WAL raises the ceiling ~10× **at the cost of a durability window** (an availability/durability, not correctness-free, trade). All figures are order-of-magnitude, hardware-dependent.
- **Redis numbers** assume single-instance, single-threaded command execution (Redis 6+ I/O threads parallelize *network only*, not command exec). Cluster spreads **different** keys across nodes, never a single hot key.
- **`C` (concurrency)**, via `C = λ·T_service`, is what drives contention — a low-`λ` but high-`T_service` workload can still be contended.
- **Balls-in-bins** shard analysis assumes ~uniform shard selection; **skewed selection reintroduces hot shards** (e.g., server-id sharding with one dominant server).
- **Network RTT** dominates unpipelined remote calls; local app aggregation removes it (and is the only thing that scales past ~10⁶/s on one logical counter).
- **Read/write ratio** governs shard count: sharded read cost is O(N); if reads ≫ writes, keep N modest and maintain a rolled-up value rather than summing N per read.
- **Skew error `O(λδ)`** (transient, relatively vanishing) is fundamentally different from **durability loss `O(λ·fsync_interval)`** (permanent); conflating them is the most common design error here.

---

## One-line recommendation

Below ~10³/s use a **single Postgres row** (exact, durable, trivial). In the 10³–10⁵/s band, **shard Postgres** if you want exact+durable without new infrastructure, or put **Redis `INCR` in front** if you need lower read latency — but in *either* case make the durable **idempotent `likes` set (or append ledger) the system of record**, and treat Redis and any hot row as rebuildable projections. That single decision is what makes the design **correct under a Redis outage**: the outage costs freshness, never a like.

# Hot Counter Under High Concurrency: Postgres UPDATE vs Redis INCR vs Sharded Counters

## 0. Model and assumptions

Let:

- `λ` = aggregate offered increment rate (ops/s) across `M` app servers, all targeting **one logical counter**
- `S` = service time the counter's serialization point is *held* per increment
- `ρ = λ·S` = utilization of that serialization point
- Reads happen at rate `λ_r`, and "accuracy" = |displayed − true committed count| at read time (absolute), or that divided by the true count (relative)

Hardware assumptions used for the numbers below (stated so you can re-derive with your own): in-memory tuple update + WAL insert ≈ 10–20 µs; fsync ≈ 100–500 µs local NVMe/SSD, 0.5–2 ms cloud block storage; scheduler wakeup/lock handoff ≈ 5–50 µs; Redis command processing ≈ 1–10 µs/op with the event loop able to sustain ~10⁵–10⁶ ops/s per instance; network RTT app→datastore ≈ 0.2–1 ms.

The key structural fact for all three options: **a single logical counter is a serialization point**. The three designs differ in (1) how expensive one pass through that point is, (2) whether the point can be split, and (3) what the failure semantics do to the count.

---

## 1. (a) Single-row atomic `UPDATE ... SET n = n + 1` in Postgres

### Throughput derivation

The subtle point most analyses miss: **Postgres holds the row-level exclusive lock until COMMIT, not until the end of the UPDATE statement.** So if each increment is its own transaction (the normal web-app case), the lock hold time is:

```
S_row = t_update (tuple + WAL insert, in memory)  ~ 10–20 µs
      + t_commit                                   (depends on synchronous_commit)
      + t_handoff (wake next waiter)               ~ 5–50 µs
```

- With `synchronous_commit = on` (default, durable): `t_commit` includes the WAL flush. Group commit does **not** help here — group commit amortizes fsync across *concurrent* committers, but transactions queued on the *same row* are not concurrent; they commit one after another. So `S_row ≈ 0.15–2 ms` and the ceiling is

  **`λ*_a = 1/S_row ≈ 500 – 5,000 increments/s`** (≈1–2k/s on typical cloud storage).

- With `synchronous_commit = off` (bounded-loss mode): `S_row ≈ t_update + t_handoff ≈ 20–70 µs`, ceiling **≈ 15k–50k/s** — but see the degradation term below.

Queueing behavior as contention rises: treating the row as an M/D/1 server, mean queue wait `W ≈ ρ·S/(2(1−ρ))`. Latency is fine at ρ=0.5, doubles by ρ=0.7, and diverges hyperbolically as ρ→1. This matters operationally more than the raw ceiling: each waiter **is a Postgres backend holding a pooled connection**. At λ = λ*, the waiter count grows without bound → connection pool exhaustion → *unrelated* queries stall. A hot row doesn't just cap the counter; it can melt the whole database tier. Design threshold: keep `λ ≤ ~0.5–0.7 / S_row`.

**Non-stationary ceiling (MVCC bloat).** Every increment writes a new tuple version and leaves a dead one. λ dead tuples/s on one hot page: HOT updates keep this on-page while there's free space, and single-page pruning cleans up opportunistically, but under sustained multi-kHz pressure the page fills, updates go non-HOT, index entries churn, version chains lengthen, and `t_update` itself grows → **throughput degrades over time**, a positive feedback loop. Mitigation (`fillfactor ≈ 50` on the counter table, aggressive autovacuum) delays but doesn't remove this. So the honest statement is: `λ*_a` is 1–2k/s durable **and decaying under sustained load**.

### Accuracy

Exact, always. MVCC readers never block on writers; a `SELECT` sees the last committed value. Error = 0, independent of λ. This is the option's entire virtue.

---

## 2. (b) Redis INCR

### Throughput derivation

Redis is a single-threaded event loop; `INCR` is O(1) on an in-memory integer. There is **no per-key contention penalty at all** — every command on the instance serializes through the loop anyway, so a hot key is indistinguishable from spread keys until the *instance* saturates:

**`λ*_b ≈ instance command budget ≈ 10⁵–10⁶ ops/s`** (per-connection rate is RTT-bound at `1/RTT ≈ 1–5k/s`, so you need many connections or pipelining to reach it).

Two caveats that bound this in practice:

1. **Redis Cluster does not shard a single key.** One hot key lives on exactly one node; adding cluster nodes adds zero capacity for it. Past ~several 100k/s on one key you are forced into option (c) at the Redis layer anyway (client-side sharded keys `cnt:{item}:0..N-1` — deliberately *without* hash tags so they land on different nodes, which means the summing `MGET` must be split per node).
2. Bandwidth/CPU of that one node is shared with everything else on it; a viral key can starve co-tenants ("hot shard" problem).

### Accuracy — the part that's usually glossed over

Redis reads are exact *with respect to acknowledged increments*, but the acknowledged count and the true count diverge under failures, and the divergence **scales linearly with λ**:

| Failure | Count error |
|---|---|
| Crash with AOF `everysec` | lose up to `λ × 1 s` increments (at λ=100k/s: 100k likes) |
| Crash with RDB only | lose `λ × minutes` |
| Failover (async replication) | lose `λ × replication lag` |
| Client timeout + naive retry | **overcount** ≈ `λ × P(ambiguous outcome)` — INCR is not idempotent, and a timed-out INCR may or may not have applied |

So "Redis is exact" is only true in the failure-free path. Its steady-state error is 0 but its **incident error is Θ(λ)**, unbounded in advance unless you bound it architecturally (§5). Note the symmetry: Postgres with `synchronous_commit=off` has loss window ≈ 3×`wal_writer_delay` (~600 ms default) — i.e., async-commit Postgres is in the **same durability class as AOF-everysec Redis**, just 10–50× slower. That's a fair like-for-like comparison; comparing durable-PG throughput against volatile-Redis throughput is the classic apples-to-oranges benchmark sin.

---

## 3. (c) Sharded / approximate counters

### Throughput derivation

Split the counter into `N` sub-counters; each increment picks one (random, or hash of server/thread id — random gives per-shard rate `λ/N` with binomial fluctuation; per-server hashing gives cache locality but risks imbalance). Per-shard utilization drops to `ρ/N`, so:

```
λ*_c(N) = min( N × 0.7/S_row ,   ← per-shard serialization, keep ρ_shard ≤ 0.7
               X_wal_group,       ← shared WAL flush bandwidth
               X_cpu, X_conn )    ← per-node resources
```

Crucially, sharding **restores the benefit of group commit**: transactions on *distinct* rows can overlap and flush together, so the WAL term is `K/t_fsync` (K = txns per flush group) ≈ 10⁵/s-scale, far above the single-row ceiling. Throughput is ~linear in N until a shared resource binds — in Postgres typically CPU/connections at tens of thousands of TPS, in Redis the per-node loop.

Choose **`N = ceil(λ_peak × S_row / 0.7) × safety(≈2)`**. Example: λ_peak = 20k/s durable PG, S_row = 0.5 ms → N ≥ 29 → use 64. Implementation detail that actually matters: put shards on **separate heap pages** (fillfactor, or padding), otherwise you've traded row-lock contention for buffer content-lock contention on one page and gained less than N×.

Diminishing returns: reads cost O(N), and N beyond ~64–256 buys little because you've hit the shared-resource terms anyway.

### Accuracy derivation

- **Sum-on-read in one Postgres transaction**: MVCC gives a consistent snapshot across all N rows → the sum is *exact at a point in time*. Sharding in PG costs **zero accuracy**. (Underrated property.)
- **Sum across Redis nodes / non-snapshot reads**: the N GETs happen over a time spread `t_spread`; the sum corresponds to no single instant, skew bounded by `λ × t_spread` (small: ~λ × few ms).
- **Cached sum with TTL τ** (you will want this — O(N) reads at high `λ_r` are wasteful): staleness ≤ `λ × τ` absolute. Relative error = `λτ / C(t)`; since a viral counter's total C grows ∝ λ·t, relative staleness ≈ `τ / age` — after 10 minutes with τ=1 s, ≤0.2%, imperceptible.
- **Buffered/approximate variant** (per-app-server in-memory accumulator, flushed every δ as `UPDATE ... SET n = n + $delta`): write rate to the store collapses from λ to `M/δ` statements/s **independent of λ** (M=200 servers, δ=1 s → 200 stmt/s — trivial even nearly unsharded). Cost: staleness ≤ λδ, and **crash loss ≤ one server's buffer = (λ/M)·δ**. This is the only design whose DB load is O(1) in λ; it's how every large-scale like-counter actually works.

---

## 4. Crossover points (with the assumptions that produce them)

Assumptions: durable writes wanted at the store of record; cloud SSD fsync ≈ 0.5 ms; design to ρ ≤ 0.7; 5× headroom for virality spikes (a counter that's hot is, by definition, one whose λ you failed to predict).

| Sustained λ (peak ÷ headroom) | Cheapest correct design | Why the previous one fails |
|---|---|---|
| < ~200–500/s | (a) plain PG row | — (this covers 99.9% of "hot" items; don't over-engineer) |
| ~500/s – ~10–20k/s | (c) N=16–64 sharded PG rows, snapshot-sum reads | single row hits `1/S_row`, waiter pileup exhausts pool, bloat decay |
| ~20k – ~200k/s | (b) Redis INCR for display **+** (c)-buffered flush to PG for truth | even sharded PG binds on CPU/connections; per-write RTT×connections cost |
| > ~200–500k/s | client-sharded Redis keys + per-server buffering (b+c), or a log/stream aggregator (Kafka→rollup) | single Redis key = single node saturates; cluster can't split a key |

Accuracy scaling with contention, side by side:

- (a): error **0**, independent of λ — pays for it with a hard, decaying throughput ceiling and blast-radius risk.
- (b): error 0 in steady state; **incident error Θ(λ × loss-window)**, plus Θ(λ × p_timeout) overcount if retries are naive.
- (c): error bounded and *chosen by you*: ≤ λτ (read cache) + λδ/M per crashed server (buffering); with PG snapshot sums and no buffering, exactly 0.

One more honest reframing: if a "like" is unique per user, the counter is really `|{users who liked}|` — a set cardinality, not an integer. That makes an idempotent per-user ledger (below) the *natural* representation, and makes INCR-style counting structurally prone to drift (retries, un-likes). Exact dedup requires the ledger; HyperLogLog is only relevant if approximate distinct-count were acceptable (for likes it usually isn't, since un-like must decrement).

---

## 5. Recommended policy — correct under a Redis outage

**Principle: Redis is a derived cache, never the system of record.** Any design where the authoritative count exists only in Redis is *not correct under outage*, full stop: crash/failover loses an unknowable delta, and ambiguous INCRs make the surviving value untrustworthy in both directions. The common anti-patterns to reject explicitly:

- ✗ "INCR in Redis, cron persists the value to PG" — outage loses the un-persisted delta and you can't tell how much.
- ✗ Dual-write (PG + Redis, both authoritative) without an outbox — they silently diverge; you now have two wrong numbers.

### The policy

**Source of truth (Postgres), write path:**
1. Each like is an **idempotent ledger insert**: `INSERT INTO likes(item_id, user_id) ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`. Insert-only, no hot row; retries are safe (idempotence solves the ambiguous-outcome problem *by construction*, which no counter representation can). Index the unique key in an order that avoids rightmost-leaf pileup for one item (e.g., `(item_id, user_id)` is fine since user_id spreads within the item).
2. A **single-writer rollup job** (or per-shard writers) periodically folds new ledger rows into `item_counts` — one writer per shard ⇒ zero contention on the materialized counter, and it also handles un-likes. If write rates exceed what ledger inserts can take, interpose per-app-server buffers with δ ≈ 0.5–1 s flushes (accepting loss ≤ (λ/M)·δ per server crash, or WAL the buffer locally if even that is unacceptable — state which you chose).

**Display path (Redis as accelerator):**
3. Redis holds the display value. App servers `INCR` it **fire-and-forget behind a circuit breaker** for real-time feel; the value is periodically **overwritten** (`SET`, with an epoch tag) from the PG rollup, so any INCR drift (retries, missed increments during blips) is bounded by one refresh interval and then corrected. Redis errors never fail the user request.

**Under Redis outage (the correctness argument):**
4. Writes are unaffected — the ledger is PG. **Nothing is lost.**
5. Reads fall back to `item_counts` (+ optionally the recent ledger delta), fronted by **request coalescing / single-flight** so the stampede of display reads becomes ~1 PG read per item per second, not λ_r. Displayed value is stale by ≤ rollup interval — degraded freshness, never wrong data.
6. **Recovery:** never trust the surviving/replica Redis value. Repopulate with `SET` from PG, epoch-guarded so a late INCR from the old epoch can't resurrect a stale count. Clamp the *displayed* value per item to max-seen (or rely on the epoch) so users never watch the count go backwards across a failover.

**Why this dominates:** it takes (a)'s exactness where it belongs (system of record, via an idempotent representation immune to hot-row contention), (b)'s throughput where it belongs (display path, where an error bounded by one refresh interval is invisible), and (c)'s O(1)-in-λ database load (buffered/rolled-up writes) — while making the Redis outage a *freshness* incident instead of a *correctness* incident. The residual approximations are explicit and bounded: display staleness ≤ refresh interval + λτ, and (only if you enabled server-side buffering) crash loss ≤ (λ/M)·δ per failed server.

# Hot counter: contention-vs-throughput-vs-durability trade-off

## 0. One lens for all three (common frame)

Every strategy has exactly one *serialized resource*. Model it as a single-server queue: service time τ, ceiling 1/τ, and latency that blows up (Little's law) as offered load λ·τ → 1. The three designs differ only in **what serializes** and **whether the fast path is durable**.

Symbols: λ = increment rate to the ONE key (ops/s); ρ = read rate; r = ρ/λ; N = shards; f = commit fsync latency; RTT = round trip; D = durability requirement (may we lose the last few increments on a crash?); S = tolerable display staleness. **All numbers below are order-of-magnitude and hardware/config-dependent — the load-bearing result is the *relations*, not the digits.**

---

## (a) Single-row Postgres — `UPDATE counters SET n=n+1 WHERE id=k`

**Serialized resource:** the row lock on tuple k, held until the transaction commits; a durable commit waits on the WAL fsync. Writer B cannot acquire the lock until writer A has committed and released it, so same-row writers form one FIFO queue:

> **τ_pg ≈ t_lock_handoff + t_exec + t_commit ⟹ ceiling μ_pg0 ≈ 1/τ_pg.**
> Durable, `synchronous_commit=on`: **~10²–10⁴ ops/s** (spinning disk ~100/s; SATA SSD ~1–2k/s; NVMe ~3–10k/s; synchronous replication pulls it lower). `synchronous_commit=off` raises the raw rate to ~10⁴–10⁵/s but drops durability of the recent tail (violates D=yes).

**Two things a shallow pass gets wrong:**

1. **μ_pg0 is essentially independent of app-server/core count.** Adding servers only lengthens the same queue → higher latency, flat throughput.
2. **MVCC makes the cap time-dependent, not static.** Each UPDATE leaves a dead tuple. An unindexed counter column enables HOT updates + opportunistic page pruning (partial self-heal) *until* fillfactor headroom is exhausted faster than autovacuum reclaims it; then updates migrate off-page, version-chain/heap cost climbs, and *sustained* throughput droops below peak. Treat it as a **decaying cap gated on autovacuum keeping pace**, not a flat line.

**Honest nuance on group commit (this is where a blanket "1/fsync" claim is too strong):** group commit amortizes fsyncs across *concurrent, distinct* committing transactions. For the **same hot row** there is nothing to batch — B hasn't started when A commits — so group commit does **not** rescue the single-row ceiling. But the exact figure still depends on `synchronous_commit`, `commit_delay`, and WAL settings, so state μ_pg0 as "≈ one durable commit latency" rather than a hard constant.

**Read accuracy:** exact + durable, O(1).

---

## (b) Redis `INCR`

**Serialized resource:** the single-threaded command loop. INCR is O(1) in RAM (~µs); persistence is off the hot path. RTT is the naive per-connection limit (~1/RTT), but **pipelining/many connections amortize RTT** toward the CPU rate:

> **μ_redis ≈ 10⁵–10⁶ ops/s.** Ratio to μ_pg0 spans roughly **10×–1000×** (honestly: (10⁵–10⁶)/(10²–10⁴)); "orders of magnitude, not 2×" is the robust claim, ~100× a defensible midpoint.

**Durability — corrected to avoid over-claiming.** Redis is *not inherently* a lossy store: `appendfsync always` (or `WAITAOF 1 0 0`) fsyncs each write and *can* make INCR durable. **But that re-imposes an fsync per op and collapses μ_redis back into the disk-bound Postgres regime — you re-buy exactly the cost that made Postgres "slow."** In its *fast* configurations (RDB, `appendfsync everysec`, async-replica failover), Redis is **exact-but-volatile**: a crash/failover loses a bounded recent window (snapshot gap / ~1 s / replication lag). So the accurate statement is: *Redis's ~100× edge and its durability are mutually exclusive at the config level*; you pick one. Speed ≠ correctness.

**Read accuracy:** exact-in-RAM, O(1), with a recoverable-loss window equal to its fsync/replication lag.

---

## (c) Sharded counters (N sub-rows, summed on read)

**Contention:** uniform-random shard selection gives each shard load λ/N — each shard is the single-row problem at 1/N load. No shard saturates while N > λ·τ_pg. Aggregate write ceiling rises **~N·μ_pg0 (linear)** *until a shared resource bites*:

> **μ_shard ≈ min(N·μ_pg0, μ_WAL, pool).**

What ends linearity (name it — this is the real answer, not "N forever"):
- **WAL group-commit rate μ_WAL** — with *distinct* rows the commits ARE concurrent, so group commit now works and batches fsyncs. This makes μ_WAL the true durable ceiling (high, because fsyncs are batched), reached at modest N; the pure linear-in-N region is therefore narrow and transient.
- **Heap-page / buffer-lock false sharing** if shard rows co-locate → set `fillfactor` so shards sit on distinct pages.
- **Connection-pool** concurrency width.
- **Hot shard from skewed hashing** — balls-in-bins max load ≈ λ/N + O(√(λ log N / N)); small *only* under uniform hashing. A skewed hash re-creates the bottleneck. Shards needed to escape contention: **N ≳ λ/μ_pg0** (e.g. λ=10⁵, μ_pg0=10³ → N ≳ 100).

**Read cost & accuracy — corrected.** An exact read is `SELECT SUM(n)` over N rows = **O(N)**. Crucially, a **single SQL statement runs under one MVCC snapshot even at READ COMMITTED** (READ COMMITTED takes a fresh snapshot *per statement*, not per row) — so the sum is **point-in-time consistent as of one snapshot, with NO cross-shard skew**. The only error is *staleness* ≤ query duration. Cross-shard **skew appears only if you read shards with separate, non-transactional gets** (N distinct queries, or MGET across Redis nodes), bounded by λ·(read span) and converging to exact when writes quiesce. (This corrects a common mistake that attributes per-row skew to READ COMMITTED.)

---

## Disambiguating "accuracy" (the word hides four things)

1. **exact-durable** — Postgres single-row / sharded.
2. **exact-volatile** — Redis INCR (loses a bounded recent window on crash).
3. **exact-sum-with-read-skew** — sharded read via *separate* per-shard gets (skew ≤ λ·read-span; zero for a single SUM statement).
4. **probabilistic-ε** — Morris counters (bounded *relative* error, tiny space) / HyperLogLog (unique cardinality, std err ≈ 1.04/√m).

**For a user-facing like count the answer is (1)/(2)/(3).** Morris/HLL are a **red herring here**: they save *storage* when exact counts don't fit, but a like count is 8 bytes — storage is never the constraint, and users would see a visibly wrong number. HLL is a legitimate but *different* answer only if "likes" means *unique likers*. The "approximate" in "sharded/approximate counters" means sense (3), not Morris.

---

## Crossovers (as inequalities, each with its assumption)

Let μ_pg0 = 1/τ_pg.

- **R1 — λ ≲ 0.7·μ_pg0 (≈ a few ×10³/s durable) and D=yes → plain single-row Postgres.** Simplest, exact, durable; sharding/Redis are needless complexity. *Assumes:* modeled fsync latency and autovacuum bounding hot-row bloat. **Most "viral single items" actually live here** — likes to *one* item rarely exceed a few k/s.
- **R2 — μ_pg0 < λ < μ_WAL and D=yes → sharded Postgres**, N ≈ (λ/μ_pg0)×(2–4). *Assumes:* uniform hashing (no hot shard), distinct pages, WAL/pool not yet saturated.
- **R3 — λ beyond the sharded/WAL ceiling, sub-ms writes needed, and a recent-loss window ≤ D tolerable *at the display layer* → Redis INCR in front of a durable store.** *Assumes:* fast-config Redis (~1 s loss) acceptable for the *live display*, with a durable backstop holding truth. **⚠ See the crux below — R3 is where the analysis has a genuine tension.**
- **Optimal N:** total row-work ≈ λ(1 + r·N). On-demand O(N) SUM reads make sharding a **net loss when r (reads/writes) is large** — and for a viral item reads (views) ≫ writes (likes), so the feasible band 2λ·τ_pg ≤ N ≤ read_budget/(ρ·t_read) **can be empty**. **Fix: keep N sub-counters for writes but serve reads from a cached/materialized rollup total refreshed every ≤ S**, making reads O(1) and *decoupling read cost from N*. Then push **N\* = min((λ/μ_pg0)·margin, μ_WAL/μ_pg0, pool)** — beyond N\* extra shards only add rollup cost.

**Highest-leverage move, orthogonal to a/b/c — write coalescing.** Each app server keeps a local delta and flushes `+K` every ~100 ms, cutting the *store-facing* rate by factor K. This is often bigger leverage than the store choice, and — as the next section shows — it is what makes a durable store survive high λ. Cost: added staleness ≤ flush interval; loss ≤ un-flushed local delta if an app server crashes (keep the interval small or spill to a durable queue).

---

## Recommended policy — correct under a Redis outage

**Load-bearing principle: the durable authoritative ledger is Postgres; Redis, if present, is strictly a read accelerator / write absorber, never the source of truth.** This makes correctness-under-outage almost trivial: writes never *depend* on Redis for durability.

**Make increments idempotent so replay/retry can't double-count — and do it without an O(events) dedup tax where possible:**
- **For likes (the stated case), idempotency is free.** Model a like as set membership: `INSERT INTO likes(user_id, item_id) ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`. The unique key makes double-submits and replays no-ops *by construction*; the count is the rollup of that set (maintained sharded aggregate or `COUNT(*)`). You are storing membership anyway (to allow "unlike" and block double-likes), so there is **no extra dedup cost** — the append-per-event is inherent to likes, not added by this design.
- **Honest caveat:** this "free idempotency" holds only for the set-membership / like-once model. A *generic non-idempotent +1 event* needs an explicit idempotency key + dedup table, which **is** O(events) storage and a real per-increment cost — that cost would move the throughput regime boundaries and must be budgeted, not waved away.
- **Also honest:** a pure grow-only membership set (G-Set) does not model *unlike/removal*. If likes can be retracted, use a PN-style pair or an append-only signed event log — the "conflict-free" claim covers like-once, not toggling.

**Write / serve / outage / recovery:**
1. **Write path:** land durably in Postgres first (directly, or via a durable outbox/log), then update Redis (write-through). A Redis-only increment must never be the sole record.
2. **Serve path:** reads hit Redis's O(1) cached total; Redis is periodically reconciled/warmed from the Postgres rollup.
3. **Redis DOWN:** writes still commit to Postgres (truth preserved); reads fall back to the sharded SUM / cached rollup — correct, just staler by ≤ S. No loss (durable), no double-count (unique key).
4. **Redis RECOVERS:** rebuild its cached total by **recomputing the Postgres SUM** — idempotent, no delicate cross-store merge.

**Two designs to explicitly reject** (both were flags in verification):
- *"Redis-is-truth, lazy flush to DB"* — the un-flushed delta vanishes on a Redis crash = silent loss.
- *The fragile cross-store live formula* `read = PG_total + current_Redis_delta` **with a non-atomic flush** (there is no 2PC across the two stores): moving a delta D across stores creates a window where either PG has D while Redis still holds D (double-shows, then drops → non-monotonic) or Redis is zeroed before PG commits (dips → non-monotonic). **Do not promise monotonicity through a cross-store delta merge.** Recompute-from-durable-SUM on recovery avoids the whole problem — hence it is the recommended reconciliation.

---

## The crux you must not paper over (surviving dissent)

R3 says "use Redis when λ exceeds Postgres's durable ceiling," but the outage-correct policy requires every increment to land durably in Postgres. **These collide: at that λ a Redis outage is a *throughput wall*, not merely a latency degradation — Postgres by construction cannot absorb the full λ durably.** Redis-in-front raises the *read-serving* and *write-absorption* rate; it does **not** raise the *durable-write* ceiling.

The only honest escapes, and their costs:
1. **Write-coalescing** brings the store-facing rate to λ/K; if K is large enough that (sharded) Postgres sustains λ/K under `μ_WAL`, then correctness-under-outage holds — but *then Postgres already keeps up, undercutting the original reason to introduce Redis for durability* (Redis remains justified only for sub-ms read latency / display smoothing). Cost: staleness ≤ coalesce interval; loss ≤ un-flushed app-local delta on app crash.
2. **A durable append-log (Kafka/outbox) as the authoritative absorber**, with Postgres/rollup derived downstream. This *can* sustain very high λ durably — **but its durable append throughput is now the real ceiling and must be measured, not assumed.** It was asserted-not-derived in the source attempts; treat it as an engineering commitment to verify.
3. **Genuinely accept bounded loss** at extreme λ (fast-Redis-only for the counter) — legitimate *only if* the business truly tolerates losing the recent tail, in which case the "correct under outage" requirement is relaxed by fiat and should be stated as such.

There is no free lunch: **exactly-once durable counting at a rate no single durable store can sustain requires either coalescing, a durable log with its own measured ceiling, or an explicit decision to tolerate bounded loss.** Any recommendation that claims high λ + full durability + Redis-outage-correctness simultaneously, without one of these, is overselling.

---

## Verdict (regime-dependent, falsifiable — not "just use X")

- **λ ≲ ~10³/s durable → one Postgres row.** Done. (Where most viral single items live.)
- **~10³/s < λ < μ_WAL, durability required → sharded Postgres**, N ≈ λ/μ_pg0 with margin, uniform hashing, distinct pages, **+ cached rollup so reads are O(1)**, **+ write-coalescing** to shave the store-facing rate.
- **λ above that, sub-ms writes / heavy read fan-out, recent-tail loss tolerable on the *display* → Redis INCR in front** — always on top of the idempotent durable ledger, reconciled by recompute-from-SUM on recovery.

Change any stated assumption (fsync latency & `synchronous_commit` → μ_pg0; RTT & pipelining → μ_redis; uniform hashing & page isolation → linear-in-N; r = reads/writes → whether O(N) reads sink sharding; the loss window you'll accept → whether Redis is even eligible; coalescing factor K → whether durability survives high λ) and the boundaries move. That parameter-dependence is the point — the deliverable is a policy keyed on assumptions, and its one non-negotiable invariant is: **a durable, idempotent store holds truth, Redis is at most a cache, so a Redis outage costs freshness (bounded by S), never a counted or double-counted event — up to the throughput wall, which only coalescing or a measured durable log can push back.**
